115.7Edge Computing and Internet of Things Technology for Enhancing Crop Yield

Revanasiddappa Bandi

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-7

7.1 Introduction

In India, agriculture is the primary source of income for most people. It has been noted that the agriculture industry has not seen much crop development over the last ten years. The declining crop rate is the reason behind the constant rise in food costs. This decline has caused more than 40 million individuals, since 2010, to fall into poverty. There are several causes that contribute to this, such as improper use of fertilizers, low soil fertility, illnesses, climate change, and water waste. Effective agricultural intervention is crucial, and Internet of Things (IoT) integration with sensor networks and machine learning (ML) algorithms provides the answer. It makes a significant contribution to making agriculture smarter and can alter the course of agricultural growth.

Three tiers are involved in IoT, including the network layer, application layer, and perception layer. The sensors and gadgets of the perception layer gather data in real time, which is then evaluated for further analysis and forecasting. The IoT network layer serves as its infrastructure to provide universal service. It points toward how the application layer and perception layer work together. The layer that integrates industry-specific technologies with the IoT is called the application layer. Nearly every industry is using IoT, including smart parking, smart buildings, smart agriculture, smart transportation, and many more. Among these, one of the major industries that affects millions of people is agriculture.

7.2 Literature Review

Patil and Kale [1] proposed a wise agricultural model in integration with information and communication technology (ICT). ICT has always mattered in the agriculture domain. Village farmers may have planted the same crop for centuries, but over a period, weather patterns and soil conditions and epidemics of pests and diseases changed. By using the proposed approach, receiving updated information allows the farmers to cope with and even benefit from these changes. It is a challenging task that 116.needs to provide such knowledge because of the highly localized nature of agriculture information, specifically distinct conditions. The complete real-time and historical environmental information is expected to help achieve efficient management and utilization of resources.

Cunningham and Holmes [2] posited that the subjective attributes for mushroom grading may not be useful in practice, and so perhaps they need not be measured or recorded. Criteria based on the attributes found in the J4.8 models may prove useful in developing more objective standards for quality classification and market pricing for mushrooms. In other data mining applications, the goal might be to use a model predictively and to provide an automated classification of new instances. In these applications, the learning component will likely be a small part of a much larger software system. As Waikato Environment for Knowledge Analysis (WEKA) learning schemes are accessible from other programs, a learning module can be slotted into a larger system with a minimum of additional programming.

Minbo et al. [3] proposed an information service system of agriculture IoT. Compared to other IoT information systems, this system can better manage and make use of the multiple sourced, real-time, and enormous data stored in distributed IoT-information servers (ISs). Meanwhile, every agricultural product is well identified and decoded to query the information of agriculture IoT with this system. All the perception data are directly associated with business data and agricultural products which can perform management and query conveniently. The tracking and tracing of the whole agricultural production process are realized with the data service (DS) server and distributed IoT-ISs. An information discovery system consists of object naming service (ONS), DS, and IoT-IS, designed to realize capturing, standardizing, managing, rapidly locating, and conveniently querying of all business data of agriculture production. A business event model of agriculture IoT is designed for unified management. In addition, for production, processing, and circulation enterprises, this system can improve productivity and strengthen enterprise management. Meanwhile, consumers can use this system to query product information to verify the authenticity and quality of agriculture products.

Mohanraj et al. [4] explained how farmers need help during different stages of crop growth and guidance should be given at the right time. Farmers are suffering a lot economically, socially, and politically. Various challenges in the agricultural domain are identified, and architecture was framed to meet the challenges mentioned above. The knowledge base is structured with various crop details that speak about knowledge acquisition, flow, various inputs like market availability, geospatial data, and weather prediction . Monitoring contains modules like reminder, monitoring plant growth in various stages, irrigation planner, crop profit calculator, calamity check, and problem identifier. The evapotranspiration method is used to calculate the water need of a plant per day with the devised algorithm’s help. A comparative study was made between various applications available with the current developed system taking various aspects into account like knowledge base, monitoring modules, efficiency, and reliability.

Sivakumar [5] explained that the sensors and microcontrollers of all three nodes are successfully interfaced with the Raspberry Pi, and wireless communication is achieved between various nodes. All observations and experimental tests prove that 117.project is a complete solution to field activities, irrigation problems, and storage problems using a remote-controlled robot, smart irrigation system, and a smart warehouse management, system, respectively. Implementation of such a system in the field can help improve the yield of the crops and overall production.

Rad et al. [6] proposed that the potato crop for future generations will require practices, processes, and systems that are sustainable (economically, environmentally, and socially). In this context, this paper presented a precision agricultural management integrated system architecture for monitoring vegetation condition of potato crop based on Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) architecture and design technologies. The proposed system allows farmers to follow the evolution of certain parameters of interest and take appropriate decisions to increase agricultural productivity. Implementing such a system is not an easy task and requires knowledge of potato crop, management strategies, processing, and visualization of information technologies to make it be viable in practice. Finally, the concept presented in this paper will represent the start of other research in the field of precision agriculture.

Chandhini [7] proposed that IoT-based agricultural production system has been built on the long-standing desire of farmers to ensure their land remains productive into the future. It also addresses the community’s expectations and concerns for safe food and environmental protection. An IoT-based agricultural production system was designed and implemented with a graphical user interface (GUI) for real-time monitoring and visualization of farm data. This system integrates IoT technology to collect, analyze, and display environmental and crop-related parameters, thereby enabling efficient decision-making in agricultural production. The IoT-based agricultural production system through correlation analysis between the crop statistical information and agricultural environment information has enhanced the ability of farmers, researchers, and government officials to analyze current conditions and predict future harvests. Additionally, agricultural product quality can be improved because farmers observe the whole cycle from seeding to selling using this IoT-based agricultural production system. The production system can be improved to support more types of products and provide more services. By taking advantage of IoT technology, the efficiency of agricultural production can be improved significantly. With constant improvement, agriculture IoT must be able to lead agriculture production to a new era.

Satyanarayana and Mazaruddin [8] described the specific application that requires soil environmental monitoring system and analysis of those problems existing in the monitoring system, and so we designed and implemented a wireless sensor network based on the soil temperature humidity monitoring system. The system rapidly realize automatic networking and real-time data acquisition, transmission, display, having the characteristics of low cost, low power consumption, flexible networking, no cabling, friendly interface, etc. Through General Packet Radio Service (GPRS) technologies and Web Services technology, we can implement the function of the data networking and remote monitoring; it shows that the system can meet the requirements of the temperature and humidity of soil environmental monitoring and unified management. In the future, we can monitor the ground water level using an appropriate sensor. Further, the research could also be enhanced to produce a system that can monitor the whole weather condition for a large area like a state or country.

118.Managave et al. [9] explained about implementation of wireless sensor network (WSN) in precision agriculture (PA). The farmers can use the system conveniently as it has a simple user interface (UI). Also, the system will keep the farmers well notified about every minute event that occurs in the field, based on which the farmer can take appropriate action [10]. The central system is the Raspberry Pi which is connected to Arduino UNO ATmega328P/Atmega16U2 (Development Board) and the clients to a router through Wi-Fi module. The router is used for the access of web pages through UI by the clients [11].

González-Amarillo and Corrales-Muñoz [12] presented the design of a greenhouse traceability model for seedling recordkeeping and tracking using IoT. The web application has been developed to control and monitor the greenhouse as well as farmers can utilize the application regarding seedling information or harvest of the products which are developed inside the greenhouse. Using this system, the usage of water can be minimized.

Josephine and Ramya [13] discussed the prediction of millet crop yield carried out using an Radio Frequency (RF) classifier and achieved 99.74% of accuracy. Different inputs like soil moisture, maximum temperature, minimum temperature, humidity, and rainfall have been used for the prediction.

Meeradevi and Mundada [14] stated about the prediction of crop yield using linear regression technique. The data is generated by using different sensors such as temperature, nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium (NPK), pH, and humidity from the actual field, and the analysis of the data is conducted. The data will be stored in a dedicated system and collected through a server to access the system.

Authors in Ref. [15] discuss how remote sensing systems are widely used in ML. The system uses sensors like pH, temperature, moisture, rainfall, and humidity and analyzes the sensor data using algorithms such as decision trees, linear regression, gradient boost (GDBoost), and RF. Out of all these algorithms, GDBoost gives the optimal yield prediction [17]. The system helps the farmer to predict the kind of crops to be cultivated according to the environmental conditions.

Priya and Yuvaraj [16] described that the system makes use of humidity, temperature, soil moisture level, and pH collected from different sensors using IoT. In addition to these, further parameters like land type, soil type, and area sown are considered during the system built. These values are fed into the GUI developed for crop prediction and provide recommendations using crop suggestion UI. A deep neural network (DNN) was used for the prediction of a crop cultivated, production range, and fertilizer used.

Narvekar et al. [18] explained that the use of IoT and WSN has revolutionized the way we collect and utilize plant information. Sensors can track and predict crop and weather conditions. Using convolutional neural networks and datasets, potato blight disease was identified, enabling automatic irrigation when soil moisture level drops and remote crop monitoring. By improving farming methods and providing cost-effective, consistent cultivation strategies, the farmers will be benefited, thus improving the agricultural industry.

Bersani and Ruggiero [19] described that the use of IoT solutions in agriculture has led to the development of smart greenhouses. These greenhouses utilize sensors and communication infrastructure to monitor and collect data in real time, enabling 119.efficient control of light, humidity, temperature, CO2 levels, and ventilation. This technology offers numerous benefits and opportunities for the agriculture industry.

Mamatha and Kavitha [20] proposed a system for hydroponics in which organic coconut coir medium is used instead of non-biodegradable rock wool. The system is automated on a large scale covering the entire greenhouse with different crops grown under optimal conditions for maximum yield. The absolute crop growth rate of leafy vegetables is predicted using the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm under various conditions. Nonfungible Token (NFT) along with coconut coir medium is found to be the best hydroponic system for commercial crop growth with an accuracy of 93%. The system produces an F1 score of 93% for weighted average and 33% for macro average.

7.3 Materials and Methods

ML is a trending technology used in the modern agriculture industry. It helps to create more healthy seeds. In ML, the methods are derived from the learning process. These methodologies need to be learned through experiences to perform a particular task. The performance of the ML model improves as it gains experience over time. Once the learning process is completed, the model can then be used to assume, classify, and test data. This is achieved after gaining experience of the training process. The motivation of the research study is to make effective developments in the agriculture sector. The study aims to predict the yield of the crop based on the type of the crop, area, climatic conditions (temperature and humidity), and pH values. The real-time data is collected through the sensors from the land using the Raspberry Pi and uploaded to the remote server. The sensory data will be fetched from the server to the integrated development environment (IDE) for predicting the yield of the crop using the ML algorithm as shown in Figure 7.1.

For PA, we have individual systems to analyze and predict crop production based on temperature, humidity, pH, and soil moisture: (1) The sensory data can be fetched through email or short message service (SMS). (2) The real-time analysis is done for monitoring plant growth. (3) Cyber surveillance is carried out for continuous alerts and monitoring.

120.7.4 Proposed System

In this research, a system is developed to predict the yield of the crop based on parameters such as temperature, humidity, pH, and soil moisture for different crops by considering different regions. For fetching data through the sensors, we have used a public application program interface (API) using the Flask framework. The real-time prediction of the yield of the crop in an area is done using ML algorithm, which is multiple linear regression. Data mining: multiple source data through comma separated value (CSV) files have been imported in predicting the yield of the crop in any area.

7.4.1 Smart Agriculture Architecture

A system architecture is a conceptual model that defines the structure, behavior, and more views of a system. An architecture description is a formal description and representation of a system. The system architecture consists of different components such as Raspberry Pi, sensors, analog-to-digital converter (ADC, MPC3008), etc. The arrow’s direction indicates the direction of the data flow. A smart agriculture monitoring and prediction system based on sensor data collection and analysis using a Raspberry Pi is shown in Figure 7.2.

7.4.2 Hardware Elements

The different hardware and sensors used in the proposed system are described in the following sections.

121.7.4.3 Raspberry Pi

The Raspberry Pi is a low-cost, credit-card sized computer that plugs into a computer monitor or TV and uses a standard keyboard and mouse. It is a small device capable of enabling people of all ages to explore computing and to learn how to program in languages like Scratch and Python. The Raspberry Pi runs Linux, but it also provides a set of general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins that allow to control electronic components for physical computing and explore IoT. Raspberry Pi 3b+ was used for the development of the proposed system as depicted in Figure 7.3.

7.4.4 Temperature and Humidity Sensor (DHT11)

DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor features a calibrated digital signal output with the temperature and humidity sensor capability. It is integrated with a high-performance eight-bit microcontroller. Its technology ensures high reliability and excellent long-term stability. This sensor includes a resistive element and a sensor for wet negative temperature coefficient (NTC) temperature measuring devices. It has excellent quality, fast response, anti-interference ability, and high performance. Each DHT11 sensor features an extremely accurate calibration of the humidity calibration chamber. The calibration coefficients stored in the one-time programmable (OTP) memory, internal sensors detect signals in the process, we should call these calibration coefficients. The single-wire serial interface system is integrated to become quick and easy. Its small size, low power, and signal transmission distance up to 20 meters enable a variety of applications and even the most demanding ones. The product is housed in a four-pin single-row pin package, consisting of a Supply Voltage (VCC), Data, Ground (GND), and one Not Connected (NC) pin, as illustrated in Figure 7.4.

122.7.4.5 pH Sensor

pH meter is an electric device used to measure hydrogen-ion activity (acidity or alkalinity) in solution. Fundamentally, a pH meter consists of a voltmeter attached to a pH-responsive electrode and a reference electrode as depicted in Figure 7.5. pH probes measure pH by measuring the voltage or potential difference of the solution in which it is dipped. Hence, a pH probe measures the potential difference generated by the solution by measuring the difference in hydrogen ion concentration using the Nernst equation and displays the pH as output.

7.4.6 Soil Moisture Sensor (Y-38 YL-69)

The soil moisture sensor or the hygrometer is usually used to detect the humidity of the soil. So, it is perfect to monitor the soil moisture of the plants. The sensor is set up by two pieces: the electronic board (at the right) and the probe with two pads, which detects the water content (at the left) as shown in Figure 7.6a. The sensor has a built-in potentiometer for sensitivity adjustment of the digital output (D0), a power light-emitting device (LED), and a digital output LED, as shown in Figure 7.6b.

The output can be a digital signal (D0) LOW or HIGH, depending on the water content. If the soil humidity exceeds a certain predefined threshold value, the modules output LOW; otherwise, it outputs HIGH. The threshold value for the digital signal can be adjusted using the potentiometer. The output can be an analog signal so that we get a value between 0 and 1023.

123.7.4.7 Analogue-to-Digital Converter (MCP3008)

The MCP3008 is a 10-bit 8-channel ADC as shown in Figure 7.7. It is cheap, easy to connect, and does not require any additional components. It uses the serial peripheral interface (SPI) bus protocol, which is supported by the Pi’s GPIO header. An ADC may also provide an isolated measurement such as an electronic device that converts an input analog voltage or current to a digital number representing the magnitude of the voltage or current.

125.126.127.128.7.6 Conclusion

131.8Intelligent Blood Bank Management Using Internet of Things for Enhanced Healthcare Delivery

Baya Reddy Lomada, B. Sreenivasulu, Anwar Bhasha Pattan, Mudassir Khan, and Shaik Karimullah

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-8

8.1 Introduction

Managing blood bags collected during donation drives requires a well-organized and efficient system as shown in Figure 8.1. Blood is essential for sustaining life, and its various components—such as red cells, plasma, and platelets—each serve a specific and critical function in the human body. Given its importance, proper storage and handling are crucial [1].

In India, the need for blood is constant, with an estimated requirement every 2 seconds. This demand is driven by a range of medical needs, including emergency treatments for accident and burn victims, surgical procedures like heart operations and organ transplants, and support for premature babies. Patients dealing with serious illnesses such as cancer, leukemia, thalassemia, and sickle cell disease also rely heavily on blood transfusions [2].

Despite having over 512 million people eligible to donate, India faces a significant shortfall—approximately 10% less than the required blood supply, which equals a gap of over 1.2 million units. To meet this challenge, there is a pressing need to boost voluntary donations and enhance the efficiency of blood bank operations.

In India, vehicle accidents occur almost every minute, often leading to severe trauma that demands immediate medical attention. Each year, the country performs nearly 60 million surgeries resulting from traumatic injuries. Additionally, there are approximately 230 million major surgeries and 331 million cancer-related procedures conducted annually, all of which contribute to the high demand for blood [3].

However, this growing need is hampered by a significant challengeIndia loses over 10 million liters of blood every day due to mismanagement and wastage. This shortfall severely affects the availability of blood units for critical treatments. To overcome this 132.issue, there is an urgent need to integrate advanced technologies into the blood management system. Leveraging digital solutions, automation, and real-time monitoring can help optimize collection, storage, and distribution, ultimately ensuring that blood reaches those in need efficiently and without delay [4].

An effective blood bank management system is vital, especially during emergencies, to streamline and automate the process of locating and allocating blood units. Such systems enable accurate tracking of blood inventories, minimizing manual errors and ensuring real-time data availability [5].

By enhancing the visibility and control over available stock, these systems help reduce wastage, ensure optimal usage of blood components, and improve accessibility for patients in urgent need. Implementing advanced and innovative management tools is essential for India to provide safe, timely, and reliable blood transfusion services across the country.

8.2 Existing System

The system integrates an embedded platform within the blood bank to continuously monitor both blood supply levels and refrigerator temperatures. It is designed to operate across two key domains: service and administration. The service domain utilizes an Arduino Mega microcontroller equipped with a Wi-Fi module, infrared (IR) sensors, and temperature sensors to collect real-time data on storage conditions and blood inventory.

This data is transmitted to the administration domain, where it is processed and analyzed. A web-based portal, hosted on a central server, provides an interface for 133.real-time monitoring and analysis. Based on the data collected, the system generates automated alerts and notifications to aid in efficient resource management, helping ensure optimal storage conditions and timely availability of blood units [6, 7].

The existing system is expected to streamline blood bank management, optimize blood utilization, and enhance blood transfusion safety and reliability [8]. Blood bank data is analyzed and processed using a website hosted on a server. This is according to notifications that are shown. On an Internet of Things (IoT) application layer, the server and blood bank securely communicate using the HTTP protocol. Maps are used to locate the designated blood bank locations for more effective functioning [9].

Disadvantages of this system are that the absence of an automated management system in blood banks leads to several issues, including difficulties in accurately tracking the inventory of each blood type [10]. The staff are not informed when the inventory level reaches zero or when blood quantity falls below par. These shortcomings can have serious consequences for patients in need of blood transfusions. Therefore, implementing an automated blood bank management system is crucial to ensure a safe and efficient supply of blood to those who require it [11].

8.3 Proposed System

The proposed system can be realized using an Arduino Uno board. One wire from four IR sensors and the DHT11 sensor (which measures both humidity and temperature) and Buzzer is connected to this Arduino Uno board, and another wire from four IR sensors and the DHT11 sensor is connected to the liquid crystal display (LCD). The LCD displays temperature, humidity, and the availability of bloodstock. The Arduino board receives the LCD connection as shown in Figure 8.2.

The results obtained on the LCD are sent to the Uno board, which stores them. The Uno board serves as the controller. The results from the Uno board are sent to the Wi-Fi and Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) modules. The GSM module alerts donors when the blood supply is low. Wi-Fi module is linked to the IoT 134.website, in this case ThingSpeak, which automatically updates the results and can be accessed from anywhere in the world.

The components of proposed system are as follows.

  1. Power Supply: Regulated power supply is essential for the optimal functioning of digital circuits. This article delves into the intricacies of obtaining a regulated positive supply from the mains supply. The process is crucial for ensuring the reliable and safe operation of digital circuits, as fluctuations in power supply can result in performance issues or even permanent damage to the circuitry. Therefore, understanding the process of obtaining a regulated positive supply is of paramount importance for individuals working in the field of digital electronics.
  2. Arduino Controller: An Arduino Uno board based on the ATmega328 microcontroller is extremely versatile and has many useful features. This device features 14 digital inputs and outputs, including six that can generate pulse width modulation (PWM) signals. In addition to universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, this device incorporates a ceramic resonator running at a frequency of 16 MHz. It offers six analog inputs. There is an in-circuit serial programming (ICSP) header, a reset button, and no future technology devices international (FTDI) USB-to-serial driver chip on this chip. Atmega16U2 (or Atmega8U2 up to version R2) serves as the serial-to-USB converter. Data transfer and communication are made easier and more efficient with this advanced technology.
  3. LCD: There are many types of LCDs, but most of them are thin and flat. In front of a reflector or light source are arrays of color or monochrome pixels. Physico-chemically, a pixel consists of a suspension of liquid crystal molecules between two electrodes. Also included are two perpendicularly polarized filters.
  4. Buzzer: Vehicles, microwave ovens, and game shows use buzzers, or beepers, for signaling. Devices typically consist of multiple switches or sensors connected to a controller.
  5. GSM Module: Mobile voice and data services are provided worldwide by GSM. Most of the time, it operates on the 900 and 1800 MHz mobile communication bands. There are three primary systems that comprise the GSM network: the Switching System (SS), the Base Station System (BSS), and the Operation and Support System (OSS).
  6. NODEMCU WIFI Module: NodeMCU is an open-source piece of firmware that runs on the ESP8266 Wi-Fi chip and is written in the LUA programming language. In addition to the Wi-Fi-enabled ESP8266 chip, this firmware is included with the ESP8266 development board/kit. An ESP8266 SoC module with TCP/IP support was created by Express Systems. Applications involving embedded IoT frequently use this technology.
  7. IR Sensor: IR light, also known as “IR radiation,” is an electromagnetic radiation. Despite being invisible, it adheres to the same principles as visible light and can either be reflected or penetrate transparent objects, such as glass. IR remote controls utilize this unseen light as a means of communication between the control and the device being controlled.
  8. 135. Humidity Sensor: Humidity sensors are becoming increasingly important in various measurement and control technologies. Material and machinery quality are dependent on humidity for human comfort. Several circuits rely on humidity sensors SYH2 and SYH-2S.

Advantages of proposed system are

  1. The availability of blood can be checked through a web page.
  2. As soon as the blood quantity drops below the designated threshold, an alert is generated.

8.5 Conclusion

This powerful system is developed using the IoT to address that problem, providing a technique to satisfy patients’ or victims’ needs for blood without requiring them to visit the blood bank to find out whether the blood is available. The Arduino board is connected to an IR sensor, which periodically verifies the availability of bloodstock. Anyone with access to the internet can use the Wi-Fi module to the output records from the Arduino on the homepage and see the maximum latest data.

151.9Innovative Applications for a Smarter and Sustainable FutureLeveraging the Power of Internet of Things and Machine Learning

Kishor Kumar Reddy C., Madiha Munawar, Monika Singh T., and Marlia Mohammed Hanafiah

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-9

9.1 Introduction

9.1.1 The Role of Internet of Things and Machine Learning in Smart and Sustainable Development

The Internet of Things (IoT) and machine learning (ML) synergism offers societies an unprecedented paradigm toward sustainable development. The IoT provides connectivity for devices, sensors, and systems for real-time data collection and communication, whereas ML acts on this data to provide insights, make decisions, and optimize processes. Both technologies thus permit optimum resource usage, minimal waste, and intelligent solutions for sustainability (Jaber, 2023). Whether in energy management, healthcare, or urban planning, IoT and ML drive innovation toward a smarter tomorrow. Energy efficiency is one of the major areas in which IoT and ML contribute to sustainability. In smart grids, IoT sensors monitor energy consumption in real-time, while ML algorithms predict patterns of demand and optimize energy distribution (Rahman, 2023). This reduces energy waste, allowing for better integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid, thereby promoting a sustainable and resilient power infrastructure (Revathi et al., 2024). Similarly, IoT-enabled predictive maintenance and usage of ML in analyzing the collected data helps industrial setups reduce equipment failures, which in turn minimizes energy loss while maximizing resource utilization.

In the environmental space, IoT-based sensors are tracing air and water quality, deforestation, and climate changes, over time obtaining valuable data that will act as a lever for conservation (Hiran et al., 2021). Pollution trends become decipherable 152.as these data are analyzed with ML models, while environmental hazards will be forecasted and landfilling processes optimized. Another important area is smart agriculture, where an IoT-based monitoring system is used to determine soil health, automate irrigation, and improve crop yield, which helps secure food and mitigate environmental threats (Shaik et al., 2024).

Figure 9.1 represents the architecture of the IoT system and ML. It also highlights the interaction among IoT devices, gateways, and the cloud. At the base of the IoT architecture are various IoT devices—smart home appliances, connected vehicles, wearables, and industrial sensors—which communicate through wireless networks. Such a device will transmit data to the IoT gateway, which will act as an intermediary to process and filter the data before transferring it into the cloud. The IoT clouds would serve as the central hubs for the data storage, analytics, and decision-making purposes. This architecture can provide very clear communication between all smart devices and can enhance automation, remote monitoring, and real-time data processing of various applications such as smart homes, transportation, healthcare, and energy management. In fact, their role in smart environments extends beyond singular applications, forging ecosystems that are intelligent and self-sustained. Such technology allows for instantaneous adaptation, automation, and seamless integration between infrastructure, transportation, energy, and healthcare, allowing smart and sustainable development to remain a tangible goal. Their full potential could be achieved if challenges posed by data privacy, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based ethics in decision-making were addressed.

9.1.2 Importance of Innovation for a Smarter Future

Innovative capability is the key to building smarter, more effective, and more sustainable systems. As the population expands and urbanization multiplies at an unprecedented rate, the demand for intelligent solutions continues to develop, considering the most important aspects of resource allocation efficiency, productivity maximization, and environmental degradation minimization (Von Stamm & Trifilova, 2009). The 153.latest technologies, such as the IoT, ML, AI, blockchain, and even fifth-generation (5G) technologies, are bound to change the way industries run, enhance public services, and thereby contribute to the making of smart cities and sustainable infrastructure. One very important facet of innovation for a smarter future is the automation and digitalization of industries. Smart factories depend on IoT-instrumentation sensors and AI-driven robotics to optimize production lines, reduce defective products in their production, and increase quality checks (Schaffers et al., 2012). Similarly, the public transport system is improved by connected, automated vehicles and AI traffic optimization and thus reduces both traffic congestion and fuel and carbon emissions. In this way, it helps increase efficiency in creating cleaner environments. Technological advancements in IoT and ML within the healthcare industry are transforming how patient care is being delivered by enabling real-time health monitoring, predictive diagnostics, and personalized treatment plans (Han & Hawken, 2018). The wearable devices are being used to capture real-time physiological data, which are being processed using algorithmic AI for anomaly detection and dire warnings, hence reducing hospital stays. Promotion of innovation finds its rightful place to meaningfully impact the future accessibility, hospitalization rates, and state of well-being of the individual it serves.

9.1.3 Challenges in Achieving Sustainability through Technology

Even though IoT and ML have the potential to reshape the world, it is still very challenging to make technology sustainable. Foremost questions popped in the minds of everyone and especially in the engineering field concerning the privacy and security of data (Bambam & Gajrani, 2023). The connecting point between IoT devices is the fact that they have extensive personal and operational data flowing in different channels and stored continuously. Hence, their security against cyber threats is core as they expose sensitive information and vulnerability in critical infrastructures because of breach attacks (Jayachandran et al., 2022). Therefore, possible solutions to mitigating these risks include putting up strong encryption methods, developing an AI-powered cybersecurity solution, and formulating robust data governance policies.

Additional challenges are large-scale energy consumption related to IoT deployments and AI processing. Although they conserve energy through their optimal consumption, these advanced technologies also demand a lot of power for computation, especially during model training. Specific examples, except for oil companies and automobiles, are data centers that consume most of the electricity for all other AI systems. Developing energy-efficient algorithms, using edge computing for processing instead of relying on centralized cloud services, and using renewable energy sources in AI infrastructure would go a long way toward ensuring that such advancements do not worsen the environmental dilemma (Izatt et al., 2014). Developing countries often do not have either the financial or technological infrastructure to deploy IoT and AI solutions on a grand scale. This can only be overcome through global cooperation, investment in smart infrastructure, and knowledge-sharing initiatives. If not, excluded underprivileged regions will only see the burdens of sustainability-focused innovations left in the remit of advanced economies (Abdoh, 2024). The development 154.and deployment of these technologies must also, in the last instance, address the ethical and regulatory issues for responsible development.

9.2 Fundamentals of Iot and Ml

9.2.1 Overview of IoT

The IoT can be defined as a huge network of interlacing devices, software, and sensors for real-time data collection and exchange (Abdul-Qawy et al., 2015). The devices include appliances from smart homes and industries, and they automate, enhance efficiencies, and provide decisions through remote monitoring and control. IoT systems embody wireless communications, cloud computing, and edge processing, managing seamless transmission of data (Gupta & Quamara, 2020). With the increasing demand for IoT, healthcare and agriculture sectors, as well as cities with smart facilities, experience and profit from optimal management of resources, improved operational efficiency, and foresight enabled through predictive analytics.

Real-time monitoring and predictive maintenance are two major benefits that the use of IoT can bring about. The presence of sensors embedded in equipment makes it possible to report to the maintenance department potential defects in machines before occurrence (Swathi Sree et al., 2025). Such facilities available in smart cities daily collect information, such as data on energy use, movement of traffic, and other waste management systems, for optimized use of resources (Dudhe et al., 2017). Precision farming that uses IoT provides information to farmers, helping them learn about the moisture content of soil, weather conditions, and crop health. This is a potential agriculture sustainer and booster to yields (Villamil et al., 2020). The IoT faces its own array of challenges, along with its advantages: these challenges include data security, interoperability, and energy consumption (Rangarajan et al., 2025). As IoT devices continuously exchange sensitive information, protecting it as well as immunity from threats become paramount. There is also the hindrance that the presence of different communication protocols does not develop a seamless integration into the different IoT ecosystems. These would include strong cybersecurity mechanisms, regulatory framework enhancement, and development of energy-efficient architectures for IoT (Albreem et al., 2017). While the technology progresses, overcoming these challenges becomes vital for the role IoT will play in driving smart and sustainable development.

9.2.2 ML: Key Concepts and Techniques

ML is a subset of AI that allows computers to learn from data and gradually improve their performance without being explicitly programmed. It uses statistical techniques and algorithms for discovering patterns, predicting behaviors, and optimizing decision-making (Zaki et al., 2020). In general, ML techniques can be classified into these three primary categories: supervised learning, in which models learn from labeled data; unsupervised learning, which finds hidden structure in unlabeled data; and reinforcement learning, where agents learn how to operate in an environment to maximize their rewards. These techniques are being actively applied in various domains, such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems.

155.The ML industry has enhanced automation and intelligence across sectors. ML-based diagnostic engines use medical imaging plus patient records to detect diseases early and suggest personalized treatment options (Vieira et al., 2020). Fraud detection models in financial services spot suspicious transactions by analyzing patterns of user behavior. The issues surrounding ML, however, include bias in training data, interpretability, and computational burden (Jung, 2022). Unfair outcomes may arise from the training data being biased toward certain groups or against others, particularly in critical applications including hiring, lending, and criminal justice. Besides, a lot of ML models are said to work as “black boxes,” which generates difficulty in understanding the decisions made. A computationally heavy model would raise concerns over energy consumption in the first place, as many complex models entail their training through heavy processing power. Hence, the solutions to these challenges should include an application of ethical AI practices, interpretable model architectures, and energy-efficient computing techniques that would provide for responsible and sustainable ML engagement.

ML concepts and techniques are presented in Table 9.1, categorized according to type of learning, algorithms used, and areas of application.

Table 9.1 ML Key Concepts and Techniques
Concept Type of Learning Algorithms Application Area
Supervised learning Supervised Decision trees, SVM, linear regression Classification, prediction
Unsupervised learning Unsupervised K-means clustering, PCA Pattern recognition, segmentation
Reinforcement learning Reinforcement Q-learning, deep Q networks Robotics, game AI

9.2.3 Synergies between IoT and ML

Owing to the architecture of the IoT combined with the revolutionary aspects of ML, automation has become a more intelligent and smarter decision-making machine industry-wise. Real-time data generated by interconnected devices through their sensing elements goes a mile toward enhancing productivity, effectiveness, efficiency, speed, resource consumption, and cost by intelligent processing, analyzing, and drawing out of meaningful insight from that data by ML techniques (Shinde et al., 2023). Smart cities leverage the combined power of IoT and ML for traffic management, urban planning, and environment monitoring. For instance, IoT-enabled 156.sensors would gather air quality information, and pollution levels would be analyzed through ML models to alert the inhabitants when some action would be most effective (Mendhurwar & Mishra, 2018). Wise transportation systems similarly employ IoT to track the movement of vehicles while using ML algorithms to predict congestion flow patterns and eliminate them. These have thus become a part of all improved efficiencies and have also contributed toward the construction of sustainable, energy-efficient models that emit less.

9.3 Smart Cities and Infrastructure

9.3.1 IoT-Enabled Smart Cities: Applications and Benefits

The smart city, enabled through IoT, enhances the urban lifestyle with connected sensor applications, real-time data handling, and intelligent automation. Through the integration of IoT technologies into public infrastructure, the governments can boost the efficiency of energy use, waste management, transport, and public safety (Bellini et al., 2022). Smart grids, for instance, monitor electricity usage and distribute it effectively to optimize overall consumption. In parallel, an IoT-based waste management system has sensors installed to recognize the fill levels in the bins for optimizing collection routes, thereby improving efficiency and minimizing environmental impact.

Figure 9.2 shows the important aspects of the smart city ecosystem which connects all other major sectors that use high technology to optimize the performance and sustainability of the ecosystem. Eight major domains consist of smart agriculture, smart infrastructure, smart city services, smart homes, smart health, smart transportation, smart industry, and smart energy. From these areas, the new technologies, trends, and processes are brought into urban living. Smart agriculture entails precision farming, key components being intelligent traffic lights, parking sensors, and real-time public transport tracking systems. All of these effectively help in keeping traffic flowing while decreasing traffic congestion (Belli et al., 2020). The live traffic data are made available to the citizens via mobile applications, which gives them the choice of taking optimal routes and thereby minimizing delays (Gupta & Singh, 2023). Also, smart city projects install connected surveillance systems, improving security, using AI-enabled analytics to recognize anomalies, and serve to decrease emergency response times (Karimullah et al., 2024).

9.3.2 ML for Traffic Management and Optimization

ML is indispensable in improving traffic management by analyzing large data sets and optimizing real-time decision-making. Traffic flow data from sensors, cameras, and global positioning system (GPS) devices are fed through ML algorithms for predicting the congestion pattern and adjusting the signal timings accordingly. Incorporating ML models from historical and real-time traffic data creates a smarter city that reduces travel times. ML-powered adaptive traffic control systems avoid stop-and-go traffic whenever possible to save on fuel usage and reduce emissions (Patil, 2022). The successful deployment of ML for traffic optimization will face 157.several challenges, including unreliable data, integration complexity, or concerns like ethics. Traffic data can be sourced by more than one site, where inaccuracies can lead to unsound predictions (Almukhalfi et al., 2024). Furthermore, integrating ML models into existing infrastructure will necessitate significant investment and expertise. Similarly, AI decision-making concerning traffic systems will need understanding of the veins of ethics to decide without discrimination for optimization benefit to any of the traffic users. It is absolutely necessary that these difficulties be addressed if the successful deployment of ML is to be achieved in traffic management.

9.3.3 Energy-Efficient Urban Planning and Resource Management

Energy-efficient urban planning is important for sustainable development; the IoT and ML converge much in optimizing the management of resources. Smart grids use IoT sensors to capture electricity demand and adapt supply dynamically, thereby eliminating the unnecessary waste of energy. These grids also facilitate real-time 158.communication between consumers and utility providers who promote efficient consumption of energy via demand-response programs. Automated building services that are compatible with smart meters handle heating, ventilation, and lighting mostly based on occupancy and time, which saves a lot of energy costs. IoT-based optimization has its application in water and waste management systems. Inside those smart water meters furnished with IoT, humans can tell when and how the water is being used and where leaks exist; and in real time, the customers can monitor and implement conservation effectively, keeping in mind usage patterns. Similar to these, AI intelligence leads to improved analytics of detecting the peak point disposal within waste collection so that it can properly streamline collection scheduling.

9.4 Sustainable Energy and Environmental Monitoring

9.4.1 Smart Grids and Renewable Energy Integration

Smart grids in modern energy distribution certainly play a very important role in integrating renewable energy sources and improving energy efficiency. The smart grid employs IoT-enabled sensors and AI analytics in the monitoring of energy consumption, prediction of the fluctuations in demand, and regulation of the power supply. Bidirectional energy flow is facilitated: unlike the traditional power grid, the smart grid allows consumers to send hazardous levels of solar or wind energy back to the system. The decentralized energy distribution mechanism optimizes energy availability, reduces pressure on fossil fuel supplies, and thus, strengthens aggregation.

ML further optimizes smart grid operations by forecasting energy demand and thereby optimizing power generation (Speer et al., 2015). Predictive models handle dynamic energy distribution with minimal wastage by exploiting historical and real-time data. Additionally, smart grids have automated demand-response schemes whereby electricity prices would vary depending on usage data to induce consumers to become flexible in their energy consumption, shifting it to non-peak hours. This aids in energy conservation, resulting in lower carbon footprints and promoting sustainability (Kataray et al., 2023). However, even with application, renewable energy generation with smart grid integration brings issues of energy storage limitation and grid stability. Solar and wind resources are intermittent, thus requiring efficient storage solutions. Besides, ensuring grid stability in the wake of decentralized power generation demands enhanced controls. Accelerating smart grids for sustainable energy management will require both governmental and industrial investments in battery storage technologies, regulatory frameworks, and AI-based optimization strategies.

The concept of virtual power plant is depicted in Figure 9.3. This refers to integrating energy sources from both conventional and renewable resources along with mobile power plants into a virtual power plant (VPP) for distributional efficiency. The VPP control room can be defined as an automated central management in terms of software and hardware used for the generation and distribution of energy. Energy into this virtual plant is fed through conventional power plants, including thermal and nuclear power plants, hydropower plants, as well as renewable sources such as wind, biogas, and biofuel, which feed sustainable energy. Moreover, electric vehicles (EVs) also play their role by acting as mobile power storage units that eventually would 159.supply energy when required. The VPP ensures an optimal energy handling system, routing energy flow across various sectors such as homes, buildings, and farms, while improving energy sustainability and efficiency.

9.4.2 IoT-Based Climate and Pollution Monitoring Systems

IoT-based climate and pollution monitoring systems provide immediate data for the analysis of the environment for proactive measures to deal with pollution and climate change. These IoT sensors collect the data with regard to air quality, temperature, humidity, and pollutant levels through their deployment in urban and industrial areas. The data that is collected is stored in cloud-based platforms where the trends, anomaly detection, and insight generation against decision-makers have been analyzed by AI algorithms. This data-driven approach allows authorities to formulate policies that target reducing environmental hazards. It monitors air quality but also looks into the internal dimensions of the water body, being managed by the IoT. Data accuracy, network reliability, and cybersecurity are some of the challenges limiting the wide adoption of IoT.

9.4.3 AI-Driven Optimization for Sustainable Resource Utilization

Resource optimization in sustainability is a cornerstone of AI implementation across different sectors for waste reduction and efficiency maximization. In the agricultural 160.sector, AI is utilitarian via its systems to analyze weather, soil condition, and crop health to maximize irrigation and fertilizer use, therefore minimizing wastage of water and chemicals due to overuse (Alharithi & Alzahrani, 2024). In a similar manner, predictive maintenance powered by AI in industries helps to avert the breakdown of machines, thus preventing losses in operational time and energy consumption. In general, these developments lead toward sustainable use of resources.

AI also enhances waste management via intelligent sorting and recycling automation. ML algorithms identify and classify recyclable materials for optimal waste segregation. Smart waste bins equipped with AI sensors track disposal patterns and schedule efficient collection routes, reducing fuel consumption and operational costs. These innovations support a circular economy, thereby keeping resources in use by reusing and repurposing prior to disposal. AI sustainability is perceived as a viable extension but is constrained by various challenges, for instance, high implementation costs and data dependency.

9.5 Intelligent Transportation and Mobility

9.5.1 IoT in Connected and Autonomous Vehicles

With the incorporation of an IoT element into transportation, it has changed how vehicles operate into intelligent, connected items. Vehicles can now virtually speak to each other, infrastructure, and central control systems through V2X communication. They now share data in real time through various sensors like GPS and through embedded systems built within them to enhance performance, road conditions, and traffic patterns used to improve road safety and navigate the broader network. The 161.whole system enhances the efficiency of buggy driving, mitigates congestion, and pushes the construction of smart transportation networks.

Most of the autonomous vehicles (AVs) are greatly reliant upon the usage of IoT-based sensors and AI to steer without the intercession of a human being. These devices, including light detection and ranging (LiDAR), radar, and cameras, work in tandem to offer a three-dimensional vision of the environment around the car to enable the identification of any obstacles, pedestrians, and other vehicles. The real-time processing of this data by the IoT platforms allows the instant decision-making by AVs to guarantee safe and smooth transportation. As it reduces the most critical factor of human error, which, in most cases, is responsible for road accidents, IoT-based automation will significantly improve road safety. However, the potential for IoT to be widely accepted into autonomous transportation faces numerous challenges, such as cybersecurity threats as well as issues with data privacy. An example is the connection in vehicles because they usually operate on wireless communication, making them very vulnerable to hacking, which can result in accidents or unauthorized control. Besides, there must be legal and ethical implications on issues of liability in case of system failures. It establishes the basis for secure deployment of IoT-driven transportation technologies concerning regulatory frameworks and advancement in cybersecurity.

9.5.2 ML for Traffic Prediction and Route Optimization

ML is the new hype in availing better traffic prediction and travel route optimization in urban mobility. Analyzing historical and real-time traffic data enables ML algorithms to predict the different congestion patterns, recognize alternate routes, and provide users with the fastest paths (Cohen & Dalyot, 2020). AI models in traffic management systems measure several parameters that include public events, construction activities, and weather conditions to change the timing of traffic lights dynamically to minimize delays. Such intelligent systems improve the flow of traffic into major metropolitan cities while also minimizing the consumption of fuel.

Apart from making cities smarter, routes of public transportation are also optimized by ML for better operations. AI algorithms analyze the passenger demand and optimally schedule the bus and train timetables accordingly in a bid to reduce waiting times while improving commuter experience. Ride-hailing services employ ML to efficiently match two people together and complete the empty trip to reduce traffic congestion in urban areas.

9.5.3 Reducing Carbon Footprint with Smart Mobility Solutions

The transportation sector contributes heavily to global carbon emissions, thereby necessitating sustainable mobility solutions to combat climate change. Smart mobility is about IoT and AI intervening to facilitate energy-efficient modes of transportation such as EVs, shared mobility, and intelligent public transit systems (Liu et al., 2023). The adoption of EVs has been trending upward by virtue of breakthroughs 162.in battery technology and charging infrastructure; meanwhile, AI is enhancing charging and battery management for EVs, thus prolonging life and boosting efficiency. AI platforms analyze commuter preferences with live traffic conditions and recommend environment-friendly travel options. Meanwhile, smart city initiatives are promoting walkable neighborhoods with integrated multimodal transport systems that encourage citizens to opt for sustainable travel modes over private cars.

9.6 SMART HEALTHCARE AND WELL-BEING

9.6.1 IoT in Remote Patient Monitoring and Wearable Devices

It is the IoT that has changed the face of monitoring vital signs and health states. In fact, it has ushered in real-time monitoring. RPM systems collect data using these sensors and use intelligent activity tracking devices, which can include anything that measures blood glucose levels, heart rates, level of oxygen in the blood, and blood pressure. This information gets transmitted to healthcare providers, who can track the condition of the patients continuously, thus being able to intervene whenever necessary. Such technology has been subsequently useful in the management of chronic conditions, removing the need for hospital visits and thus improving patient outcomes, for instance, in diabetes and hypertension management.

Wearable devices like smartwatches, fitness bands, and electrocardiogram (ECG) monitors give users personalized insights into their health while assisting doctors with making decisions based on data. Such devices detect anomalies like abnormal heart rhythms or sudden drops in oxygen saturation, which otherwise demand potential medical assistance on a priority basis. Apart from that, IoT in wearables fosters 163.elderly care through movement pattern tracking that facilitates fall detection and medication adherence, thereby extending the safety and independence of senior citizens. However, challenges related to security of data, interoperability, and regulatory compliance confront IoT health applications.

9.6.2 ML for Disease Prediction and Diagnosis

ML is transforming disease prediction and accuracy into diagnosis through early condition detection at a much higher accuracy than earlier. It examines huge datasets of medical records to find patterns that indicate the presence of diseases or enhanced disease progression. For instance, deep learning algorithms detect early-stage cancerous tumors by interpreting medical images like X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans. AI-enabled diagnostic tools complement radiologists and pathologists in improving accuracy, reducing human error, and accelerating treatment planning. Apart from imaging, ML can now assess different genetic, lifestyle, and environmental factors in the likelihood of developing a disease and enhance predictive analytics in healthcare. AI-based risk assessors can help physicians identify risk-prone individuals for future cardiovascular diseases, Alzheimer’s, and diabetes before these develop symptoms. It can then be possible to have tailored medications that ultimately may reduce or delay disease onset while at the same time improving patient results and cutting down on healthcare expenses.

Nonetheless, while implementing ML in healthcare, there is a need for well-distributed, good-quality datasets, which will guarantee unbiased and accurate predictions. Most AI models are characterized by biases mostly arising from the non-inclusiveness of certain masses in their training data. Disparities thus arise in diagnoses as well as suggestions for treatment. Additionally, there would always be regulatory approvals and ethical issues surrounding AI decision-making that must be addressed to ensure transparency and accountability. Continuous advancement in AI ethics, model validation, and collaboration between healthcare providers and AI researchers will drive the necessary trustworthy ML solutions in medical diagnostics.

9.6.3 AI-Powered Personalized Healthcare Solutions

Virtual health assistants and AI chatbots are meant to provide patients with personalized support, such as reminders for medication, dietary suggestions, and symptom tracking. By utilizing these applications with AI capabilities, routine queries can be taken care of by these assistants, providing real-time support for patients with chronic illness, hence relieving healthcare professionals to a great extent. AI-based tools designed for mental health monitor emotional well-being using natural language processing (NLP) techniques, thereby offering tailored coping skills and treatment suggestions. Healthcare provision using AI is still facing hurdles based on ethical considerations and data privacy. AI must ensure transparency in decision-making, particularly with regard to biases of any type, to provide equitable access to healthcare. In addition, encrypted health information and compliance with health regulation principles such as Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) will go a long way in maintaining trust in AI-based 164.medical solutions. In this way, an ever-evolving AI can improve patient outcomes while protecting the ethical and secure implementation of personalized healthcare systems.

As shown in Figure 9.4, an AI-based healthcare process is necessary in patient diagnosis and therapy. The process is divided into five parts: patient data collection involves compiling medical history and health parameters; data processing with AI algorithms means analyzing the patient data using ML techniques; a personalized diagnosis and treatment plan is recommended by AI; real-time monitoring means continuous health condition monitoring using wearable devices and IoT sensors; and feedback loop and improvement involves learning lessons from monitoring and improving future therapy. All of these enhance healthcare efficiency in terms of precision, time, and flexibility in real-time services for patients.

9.7 Industrial Automation and Smart Manufacturing

9.7.1 IoT-Enabled Predictive Maintenance in Industries

With the use of IoT technologies, predictive maintenance has a profound impact on industrial operations through the real-time monitoring of equipment and machinery. Conventional maintenance approaches rely on the regularity of inspections or reactive repairs that may lead to untimely downtimes or greater costs. With an array of sensors, ML, smart sensors, and smart analytics, industries are able to monitor machine performance continuously with respect to temperature, vibration levels, and energy consumption (Compare et al., 2019). By analyzing such data, predictive maintenance schemes can forecast potential failures even before they happen, thus reducing production disruptions further and enhancing the service life of the equipment.

The primary benefit, in this case, is enhanced optimization of resource utilization and reduced operational costs. AI algorithms sift through massive amounts of sensor data to detect anomalies and patterns signifying wear and tear (Kalusivalingam et al., 2020). Maintenance activities have been protecting the production lines in manufacturing plants, such that failures in robotic arms or conveyor belts are detected by predictive maintenance before causing considerable damage. The energy sector similarly uses IoT sensors such that turbines and generators detect possible onsets of mechanical stress to avert expensive failures as well as enhance operational efficiencies. Predictive maintenance implementation, however, brings a big price tag with it in terms of investment for creating IoT infrastructure, a data management system, and 165.training the workforce. Across industries, there is difficulty bringing together IoT and other legacy systems, thus requiring seamless connectivity. It is also crucial to ensure the cybersecurity of IoT-enabled devices to prevent them from data breaches and other cyber threats. However, by tackling the above challenges through very strong security for data and scalable IoT architecture, predictive maintenance will become a means of driving efficiency, sustainability, and cost savings across industries.

9.7.2 AI in Process Optimization and Quality Control

AI is revolutionizing the optimization of industrial processes, increasing efficiency while reducing waste and improving control over quality. Traditional manufacturing processes are beset by inefficiencies due to human errors, equipment variability, and the possibility of disruptions in the supply chain. Using automation driven by ML based on the skimmed data of the past and the data of the present moment, the workflows are optimized in such a way that the factories can fine-tune the parameters like speed of production, usage of raw materials, and consumption of power to achieve maximum efficiency. Quality control in manufacturing has greatly improved, thanks to computer vision-based AI that, with great accuracy, examines products for any defects. For instance, advanced image recognition algorithms will run real-time examinations of surface defects, dimensions, and assembly correctness to make sure that only products of excellent quality are on the market. For example, in the automotive industry, AI-driven quality control detects minute imperfections in car parts before they go into the market. In drug formulation and packing, AI does well to ensure the accuracy and safety of the patient.
