222.12GiwrfGini Impurity-Based Weighted RF of Intrusion Detection in Network Security and Feature Selection Using the Machine Learning Algorithms

S.V. Sugin and M. Kanchana

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-12

12.1 Introduction

The interactions between countries, companies, and people are numerous and intricate in the complex world we live in. Information and communication technologies (ICT) are mostly used to carry out those relationships. The number of malicious users looking to take advantage of system vulnerabilities has surged along with the number of devices that are online. These malicious actors can use a variety of attacks to target organizations, governments, or people. Malicious activities range from straightforward threats like spam or phishing, parameter tampering, to more sophisticated dangers like advanced persistent threats (APTs), botnets, or social engineering assaults that make use of open-source intelligence techniques (OSINT) and domain generation algorithms (DGAs) [1, 2]. Cybersecurity experts aim to help clients secure their networks, systems, and digital assets using various tools, such as intrusion detection systems (IDSs), antivirus, or firewalls. These tools produce a huge number of details on the form of network data through a variety of normal interactions and threat ones. In addition, the appropriate combination of additional activity logs and other digital evidence assets is crucial for the successful execution of the security lifecycle [3, 4]. The automatic analysis and treatment of sample data is a crucial step in the implementation of adaptive and effective defensive techniques due to the establishment of quantities of security-related information [5]. Consequently, it is exciting to use a single method that can be applied to analyze these logs to reduce tasks and support analyst’s decision-making. For such a work, our strategy involves developing parameter-free procedures [6].

In this research, we analyze and clarify the usage of an earlier approach according to compressing data [7] in a larger circumstance that includes several binary categorization issues in the present cybersecurity context. We train a machine learning (ML) 223.system that uses these features to categorize the data by utilizing the normalized-compression distance (NCD) [8] to identify a group of attributes that describe the imbalanced network data related to every issue. The generalizing of our method, which shows an integrated framework for the investigation of network data in an overall cybersecurity environment, is demonstrated by our results in various situations. Despite the fact that we do not provide the best modern solutions for every problem under consideration, we still get competitive outcomes across all disciplines.

A Gini impurity-based weighted Radio Frequency (GIWRF) model was created in our suggested method to choose the critical and appropriate attributes based on the priority level. The scores for attribute relevance were determined by using the Gini impurity criterion to partition the trees and modifying the overall weight in the Random Forest (RF) algorithm for an imbalanced distribution of classes. However, for the ML-based IDS framework, datasets were used to create the Ada Boost, gradient boosting tree (GBT), decision tree (DT), gated recurrent unit (GRU), long short-term memory (LSTM), and multilayer perceptron (MLP). Before the models are tested and trained, data engineering or data preprocessing is needed. Three processes made up the data-preprocessing phase and will be covered later in this study. However, the binary classification task’s performance to conduct the analysis, the network dataset UNSW-NB15 [9, 10], which is a relatively new set of data containing modern attack patterns.

A binary classification task using supervised ML models was carried out in this study. When the supervised ML method is tasked with classifying a discrete value as either an attack or normal instance, binary classification takes place. The study’s dataset is rather sizable and has many feature space dimensions. It is crucial to select an attribute selection strategy for removing insignificant characteristics from a huge dataset and using only the crucial set of features in both the testing and training steps [11]. The method of reducing the set of relevant data during the process of feature selection is used to create predictive models. Most of the time, improving the performance of prediction models is desired. Additionally, irrelevant features negatively impact the performance of the model. However, because the IDS handles so many data samples that have redundant or irrelevant attributes, it not only increases the computational cost but also lowers the accuracy of detecting scores [12]. By locating the relevant attributes that contain the data required for the classification method, feature selection provides remedies to several frequently occurring errors in IDS [13].

12.2 Methods and Materials

It is necessary to note that the greater portions of the earlier discussed strategies are problem-specific. The discipline is lacking a general technique that approaches all of these challenges from a similar angle, even if all of the problems described include some sort of network data analysis. In this part, a general method for extracting a group of numerical characteristics that defines a set of data using a compression-based analysis, such as the NCD, is discussed. Calculating the separation between a T text and k a set of extra texts (g1, g2, …, gk), referred to as Attribute Generator (AG), is the main goal when given a text T. This generates a vector of k numbers that indicate the text T in a k dimensional attributes space as an input for a classification 224.model [14]. However, in this research, we have utilized ML classifiers; it is important to emphasize that our method for any other classification algorithm can be used with attribute extraction.

The specific steps are as follows for a UNSW-NB15 dataset made up of data from two different classes: The data are randomly split into two groups, G and I, each of which contains m and n data. Both groups have equal numbers of datasets for the two classes, making them both balanced. The attribute generators are constructed using the first group, G. To accomplish this, k generator files with data from only one class each are created from the data in G. As a result, each class has k/2 generators. After being distinguished by the distances to the generators of attributes, the second group (I) includes the set of data that is utilized to instruct the classifiers. To get the vector, we measure the distance between every string Si in I and each of the k-attributes generators:

Si = (xi 1 ,xi 2,……,xi k) (12.1)

It is used to describe the data Si. The following equations provide the components xij of Si:

xij = D(gj ,s i ) (12.2)

where D(gj,si) denotes the reduced data about the normalized conditions between the string (si) and the generator (gj):

$D\left( {g_{j~},~s_{i~}} \right) = \frac{C\left( s_{i~|~~g_{j}~} \right)}{C\left( {~s_{i~~}} \right)}~ = ~\frac{C\left( {~g_{j}.~s_{i~}} \right) - C\left( g_{j~} \right)}{C\left( s_{i~~} \right)}~~~$ (12.3)

The dot operator is used to indicate altogether, and C(s) represents the reduced size of (s). We make use of the gzip compressor in the tests as it performs faster than other compression methods.

Once utilize the feature vectors for the full set of data in I to train a classification algorithm that anticipates the class that each item of data belongs to using an radial basis function (RBF) kernel. The scikit learn Python package is used to implement the approach, and accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) area under the measurements of the operational feature curve of the receiver are used to determine the performance of the classifiers. The performance of the ML model is based on two hyperparameters, the kernel complexity C and the width γ, which are determined in each k using the traditional fivefold cross-validation approach as defined in ref. [14]. Figure 12.1 shows the complete procedure, from the primary dataset to the final categorization.

12.3 THE NETWORK DATASET UNSW-NB15

The dataset was published in 2015 by Moustafa and Slay [15]. There are more than 2.5 million packets on a network of data adapted to replicate this dataset. This dataset 225.includes non-anomalous packets in addition to nine other types of attacks (DoS, generic, reconnaissance, shellcode, backdoors, worms, fuzzers, exploits, and analysis). As more than 87% of the packets are non-anomalous, the set of data is extremely unbalanced. 12.4 Proposed Methodology

To provide a comparison, the outcomes of the ML methods described in the familiar ML technique (DT), deep neural network (LSTM, GRU), artificial neural network 226.(MLP), and ensemble method (AdaBoost, GBT) would be used to identify intrusions over imbalanced datasets. The main objective of the research was to use an effective feature selection strategy for an unbalanced dataset. These models were trained over the datasets described in the UNSW-NB15 network dataset chapter. The recommended approach diagram is shown in Figure 12.2.

12.4.1 Coding for Categorical Features

State, Proto, and Service are the three categorical features included in the network dataset UNSW-NB15. Response coding was utilized to convert the string attributes of the UNSW-NB15 network dataset, while use of Label Encoding to encrypt the categorical features of UNSW-NB15. Each categorical characteristic in Label Encoding is determined a distinct integer value based on alphabetical sequence. In contrast, encoding techniques shows the probability that a given category of information instances belongs to a particular class. N new features for (N) class classification that insert the (P) probability of an information instance for every class, depending on the 227.category of data value, are constructed for each category. One method of presenting a mathematical expression is:

P(X | B) = P(B∩X) / P(B) (12.4)

where B stands in for the feature category and X is indicated as a class. Given that the Network UNSW-NB15 dataset has a number of categorical features, its large memory requirements prevent it from being used to modify string features.

12.4.2 Feature Scaling

The datasets include certain features whose magnitudes, units, and ranges are highly unpredictable. A few algorithms, like the MLP, make incorrect predictions because of the dataset’s high degree of variation. Additionally, it calls for plenty of computer power. In regard to normalizing the range of independent variables, one often used method is feature scaling. For some ML algorithms that determine the separation between data, feature scaling is required. Two frequently employed features of scaling methodologies in ML are standardization and normalization. In this experiment, data between the ranges of 1 and 0 were normalized using normalization or minimum and maximum scaling. The general normalization equation is as follows:

h−  = [(h−minimum(h))/(maximum(h)−minimum(h))] (12.5)

where (h−) is the normalized attributes, and h is the original attributes. The feature’s maxi and mini values are denoted by minimum(h) and maximum(h), respectively.

228.12.4.3 Gini Impurity-Based Weighted RF

RF is an ensemble classification that supports different feature significance metrics and is constructed on a number of DTs. One of them is to train the classifier to determine the score of significance. The models are developed without taking into account the possibility of an imbalanced distribution of classes in the training data, as the conventional ML classification technique anticipates that all the categories in the training data will emerge with the same relevance [16]. After the Gini impurity was measured by the classifier, i(𝜏), this attribute selection method used a weight modification method in RF to understand the compatibility of attributes with the outcomes of the asymmetric data. A split’s ability to equally entire binary class samples into two equal parts in a given node is indicated by its Gini impurity. It can be represented mathematically as follows:

i(τ) = 1 − P2p − P2n  (12.6)

where the percentages of negative and positive samples, respectively, out of the entire amount of samples (N) at node 𝜏, are denoted as pp and pn, respectively. For each node τ in the weighted trees (M) in the forest, the decrease in Gini impurity because of each optimized split ∆if (τ, M) is collected, separately for each feature. It can be expressed mathematically as:

$I_{g}\left( f \right) = \sum\limits_{M}W_{p,n}\sum\limits_{\tau}\Delta i_{f}\left( {\tau,M} \right)$ (12.7)

Allocating the weight (wp,n) characterizes an asymmetric class distribution in the ML algorithm, where Ig is the Gini significance, which describes the frequency of a related attribute (f) as a chosen for the divide and the importance of the attributes all aspects value of discriminative for the binary categorization problem.

$~~\text{Positive~class~weight,~}W_{p} = \frac{n_{n}}{N}$ (12.8) $~\text{Negative~class~weight,~}~W_{n} = \frac{n_{p}}{N}$ (12.9)

wn + wp = 1 and wp ≠ wn for data from an unbalanced class. The positive occurrences are indicated as np, and the number of negative cases is shown as (nn). The training dataset’s total instance count is N. Table 12.3 explains the pseudo code for the algorithm used to choose the features using the sklearn package. 12.4.4 Evaluation Metric

229.The objective of this experiment was to increase the proportion of accurate binary classification outcomes in the test set. Several ML performance metrics, including 230.false positive rate (FPR), precision, recall, accuracy, etc., are applied to evaluate the effectiveness of IDS based on ML [17]. However, the most frequently employed metric for assessing how well models perform in binary classification situations is the accuracy score. It is described by the equation below:

$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\left\lbrack \left( {~\mathbf{TP}~ + ~\mathbf{TN}~} \right) \right\rbrack}{\left\lbrack \left( {\mathbf{TP} + \mathbf{TN} + \mathbf{FP} + \mathbf{FN}} \right) \right\rbrack}$ (12.10)

where TN and TP denote the true negative and true positive. The amount of accurately identified assault events is known as the true positive rate. The instances that are appropriately identified as normal are counted by TN. False positive (FP), on the other hand, refers to the quantity of genuine traffic that is incorrectly categorized as an attack. The number of assaults is counted using false negative (FN) cases that are mistakenly regarded as typical instances. Fewer FN is often anticipated in the detection of incursion as it poses a greater risk than FP. Although for asymmetric information about classes, particularly when the goal is to accurately identify the assault, four additional rules, such as FPR, Recall, Precision, and F1 score are also taken into account in added to the original value determined.

  1. FPR: The ratio of the total number of negative events to the number of negative occurrences that are mistakenly labeled as positive is known as the FPR. The expression is as described below:
$\text{FPR} = \frac{\mathbf{FP}}{\left( {\mathbf{FP} + \mathbf{FN}} \right)}$ (12.11)
  1. Precision: When a model positively predicts an instance, precision measures how often the forecast is accurate to assess how well the model performs. It can be described mathematically using the equation below:
$\text{Precision} = \frac{\mathbf{TP}}{\left( {\mathbf{TP} + \mathbf{FP}} \right)}$ (12.12)
  1. Detection Rate/Recall: It measures how well the ML model detected occurrences of TPs. Recall measures the model’s precision in locating relevant data. For this reason, it is sometimes identified to be delicate or TPR. The logical equation is represented as follows:
$\text{Detection~rate/recall} = \frac{\mathbf{TP}}{\left( {\mathbf{TP} + \mathbf{FN}} \right)}$ (12.13)
  1. F1 Score: The tradeoff between recall and precision determines the ML method’s overall accuracy by accounting for both FP and FN. The following equation represents the F1 score:
231.$\text{F}1\text{~score} = \frac{\left( {2*\mathbf{Recall}*\mathbf{Precision}} \right)}{\left( {\mathbf{Recall} + \mathbf{Precision}} \right)}$ (12.14)

12.5 Results and Experiments

This research was performed in two states and considered six ML models, including the GBT, LSTM, DT, Ada Boost, GRU, and MLP. The effectiveness of ML techniques for binary categorization was assessed in the first stage, which made use of every characteristic of the network dataset UNSW-NB15. In the second stage, the binary classification was once again carried out using six models, and only 20 attributes for the network dataset UNSW-NB15 were selected based on the suggested attributes selection technique. One consistent strategy used to train all the models was parameter adjustment, which helped this experiment increase accuracy and F1 score as well as FPR value is reduced. Table 12.5 (for UNSW-NB15) shows the binary classification outcome using ML methods on the entire feature set, while Table 12.6 (for UNSW-NB15) shows the performance of similar methods using only the chosen attributes. Figures 12.3 and 12.4, which show the F1 score, accuracy, and FPR performance comparison for UNSW-NB15, provide a visual representation of the data.

That described the proposed DT's ability to identify intrusions effectively. They opted to employ a different training size employed in the proposed research.

232.233.12.6 Conclusion

This research aimed to develop and determine the ML algorithms: GBT, LSTM, Ada Boost, DT, GRU, and MLP for the binary classification challenge of IDS based on ML. On the premise that the imbalanced distribution of classes would have an impact on the attribute selection process, a GIWRF was proposed as the attribute selection procedure to choose an appropriate collection of attributes from the imbalanced datasets in UNSW-NB15. The UNSW-NB15 network dataset attributes were decreased using the feature selection technique to 20 (from 49), respectively. The model’s effectiveness in detecting the intrusion was analyzed using the metrics FPR, Accuracy, Recall, Precision, and F1 score. The entire feature set across datasets was initially used in the research. The research was then repeated, utilizing only the selected attributes that the attributes selection algorithm had extracted. For several datasets, the algorithm's performance was compared with full attribute field and with decreased attributes. The DT performed better in the network dataset UNSW-NB15 when using the attribute selection techniques.

236.13Discrimination of Power System Disturbance and Cyber-Attacks through Machine Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence

Niharika Agrawal and Sheila Mahapatra

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-13

13.1 Introduction

Machine learning (ML) plays a critical role in discriminating between power system disturbances and cyber-attacks in modern smart grids (SGs). As SGs become more interconnected and reliant on digital communication, distinguishing between natural system faults and intentional cyber threats becomes increasingly challenging. ML algorithms help detect and classify events in power systems by analyzing real-time data patterns. They can differentiate between natural disturbances such as equipment failures, line faults, or load changes and cyber-attacks, including data injection, Denial of Service (DoS), and control signal manipulation. ML models analyze features like voltage and current waveforms, frequency deviations, Load patterns, and communication network data, which help distinguish between legitimate disturbances (e.g., a short circuit) and malicious manipulations. ML models can provide real-time detection of abnormal patterns using autoencoders for detecting the deviations from normal operation and recurrent neural network (RNNs) for time-series predictions and identifying temporal anomalies. By combining data from both the cyber (network logs, user activity) and physical (sensor readings, control commands) layers, ML can detect coordinated attacks that affect both the cyber and physical systems. It can identify subtle attacks like false data injection that can be difficult to detect through conventional methods. ML tools are able to forecast and predict possible failures and cyber threats prior to their occurrence, facilitating anticipatory maintenance planning and automated response systems that isolate compromised sections of the grid. The different challenges are:

  • 237. Data Quality and Availability: Labeled data for cyber-attacks are often limited.
  • Adversarial Attacks: Attackers can manipulate ML systems if not properly secured.
  • Scalability: Managing large-scale power grids requires efficient models.

13.1.1 Major Techniques

  • Supervised Learning: (e.g., support vector machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DTs)) trained on labeled data to classify events.
  • Unsupervised Learning: (e.g., K-Means, density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN)) for anomaly detection when labeled data are not available.

  • Deep Learning: (e.g., convolutional neural network(CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTMs)) for more complex pattern recognition and time-series analysis. Figure 13.1 shows the types of learning.

Ref. [1] presents a novel approach for enhancing cybersecurity in cyber-physical production systems (CPPS) through a hybrid DL-based attack graph model. The authors focus on early-stage detection of cyber-attacks, specifically those targeting Operational Technology (OT) networks, combines Operational Technology Graph Convolutiona (GC)-LSTM and CNNs for real-time anomaly detection. It achieves an accuracy of over 96%, outperforming existing time-series anomaly detection models. It is tested using simulations of cyber-attacks like distributed denial of service (DDoS) and network reconnaissance.

13.1.2 Types of Cyber-Attacks

  • TSA: Disrupts system timing using spoofed GPS signals.
  • Denial of Service (DoS)/DDoS: Blocks or overwhelms communication channels.
  • DRA: Reuses valid data packets to deceive systems.
  • FDIA: Alters data to manipulate control systems.
  • 238. MITM: Intercepts and modifies communications stealthily.
    • Physical Attacks: They include direct interference like electromagnetic damage or RA, which manipulate system frequencies.
    • CCPA: Combine cyber and physical methods for a more destructive, synchronized attack.

The 2019 Venezuelan SG attack used both cyber and electromagnetic disruptions. Figure 13.2 shows the types of cyber-attacks.

Ref. [2] presents an ML-based intrusion detection system (IDS) designed to enhance cybersecurity in SGs. It focuses on protecting communications using International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 61850 Generic Object-Oriented Substation Event (GOOSE) critical messages for substation automation. A novel IDS has been developed for GOOSE messages using ML to differentiate between normal operations and cyber-attacks. A realistic dataset of GOOSE messages under normal operations and simulated cyber-attacks has been created for model training and validation. The vulnerabilities in GOOSE messages are that there is no built-in encryption, message integrity, or authentication mechanisms, and the protocol is susceptible to replay, man-in-the-middle, and masquerade attacks. The IEC 62351 has certain limitations, like it provides communication-level security but lacks intrusion detection mechanisms at the operational layer. Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) is an essential system used for monitoring, controlling, and automating industrial processes, including power systems. It facilitates real-time control and monitoring of electrical grids, enabling operators to manage infrastructure efficiently across vast geographical areas. This system plays a major role in ensuring the efficiency, reliability, and stability of SGs [3]. Its main functions are included in Figure 13.3. SCADA systems are a primary target for cyber-attacks. Key vulnerabilities include legacy systems, weak authentication mechanisms, lack of encryption. With the integration of remote access and IoT devices, the attack surface has significantly expanded. Various measures related to cybersecurity for SCADA systems in SGs are:

  • Network Segmentation: Isolation of SCADA networks from corporate or external Networks to minimize exposure.
  • IDS: Monitors for unusual traffic patterns that may indicate a cyber-attack.
  • Strong Authentication and Access Control: Implementing MFA and role-based access control (RBAC) for critical systems.
  • Encryption of Data in Transit: Encrypting SCADA communications using secure protocols (e.g., TLS, VPN).
  • Regular Patch Management: Updating software and firmware for addressing known vulnerabilities.
  • Plans for Incident Response: To develop and test regularly the response procedures for minimizing the downtime during a cyber-attack [4].
  • Stuxnet (2010): A malware attack targeting industrial control systems, demonstrating the potential for cyber–physical sabotage.
  • Ukraine Power Grid Attack (2015): A well-coordinated cyber-attack that disrupted power supply using malware designed to compromise SCADA system.

239.240.13.1.3 Future Trends in SCADA Cybersecurity for Power Systems [5, 6]

Ensures the integrity and immutability of critical transactions within smart grids. SCADA systems are the backbone of modern power grids, providing essential monitoring and control capabilities. However, their growing complexity and connectivity also introduce significant cybersecurity challenges. Implementing robust cybersecurity measures is essential for the system's safety and reliability, especially when confronted with changing cyber threats.

241.13.1.4 Cyber-Attacks in India

India’s power grid, a critical component of the nation’s infrastructure, has been the target of several notable cyber threats, particularly focusing on SCADA systems. These incidents underscore the vulnerabilities present in the SG’s control systems and the ongoing efforts to enhance cybersecurity measures [7].

  1. Targeted Attacks by Chinese State-Sponsored Groups: In 2021, cybersecurity firm recorded future identified a concerted campaign by Chinese state-sponsored groups targeting India’s critical infrastructure. The campaign focused on ten Indian power sector organizations. Additionally, two Indian seaports were targeted. These attacks aimed to gather information and potentially disrupt operations within India’s power grid.
  2. Attempts to Disrupt Power Distribution Near Ladakh: In early 2021, the Indian government reported two attempts by Chinese hackers to target electricity power distribution centers. While these attempts were not successful, they highlighted the persistent threats to India’s power infrastructure. Power Minister R.K. Singh stated that defenses had been strengthened to counter such a cyber-attack.
  3. Vulnerabilities in the SCADA System: Confidential data from Computer Emergency Response Team – India (CERT-IN) show occurrence of many attacks on SCADA systems. While many of these attacks have been small-scale, there is anecdotal evidence suggesting an increase in both the frequency and scale over the years. The availability of information on breaching SCADA systems on the internet exacerbates these vulnerabilities.
  4. Malware Attack on Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant: This plant experienced a malware attack in September 2019 that infiltrated its administrative network. The malware, identified as Dtrack and linked to the North Korea–affiliated Lazarus Group, was designed to collect sensitive information. While the operational network remained unaffected, this incident underscored the potential risks to critical infrastructure from cyber threats.
  5. Security Enhancements and Monitoring Initiatives: In response to these threats, GRID-INDIA has established an SOC to monitor security events and incidents across RLDCs and the NLDC. Additionally, the IT infrastructure of the NLDC has been upgraded with advanced security features. POWERGRID, another key entity, has also set up an SOC for 24 × 7 monitoring of critical assets. These initiatives aim to bolster the cybersecurity posture of India’s power grid and protect against future attacks [8].

These incidents highlight the ongoing challenges in securing SCADA systems within India’s power grid. Table 13.1 shows the description from ref. [9].

The contributions of this work are:

  1. Implementation of various ML techniques for the discrimination of power systems disturbances and cyber-attacks in a Python environment
  2. 242. Development of CM, CR, and Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROCC) for ML models.
  3. Calculation of different performance metrics, like accuracy, precision, for all the models.
  4. The implementation of XAI with SHAP and LIME methods is done for three types of classifiers.
  5. This research contributes to enhancement of reliability, safety, and efficiency of modern power systems, all of which are foundational to achieving Goal 7 of 17 SDG
  6. By leveraging ML and XAI for addressing cyber-physical threats, this research contributes to a future where energy systems are transparent, intelligent, and act as the pillars of clean and affordable energy access.

13.2 Dataset Description

Figure 13.5 illustrates the structure of the system used in this manuscript. This structure consists of Supervisory Control Systems that engage with Network Monitoring, SNORT and Syslog Systems and other Electronic Devices. G1 and G2 are the power generators, BR1 to BR4 are breakers, Line 1 and Line 2 are lines, R1 to R4 are IEDS having the capability to toggle breakers off or on. R1 manages BR1, BR2 is managed by R2, and so forth accordingly. Each IED independently manages one breaker.

243.The dataset is obtained from Mississippi State University. There are 37 scenarios in the dataset. There are eight natural events, one no event and 28 attack events, which are grouped into three classes, including binary and multi-class datasets. Table 13.2 provides the complete information.

13.2.1 Types of Scenarios

Table 13.2 Event Types and Details⏎
Typeof Event Description Impact
Short-circuit fault A power line short may happen in different places. Can lead to instability, equipment damage, or power outages.
Maintenance of line Disabling of relays for maintenance. Temporary disabling of protection on the linae, increasing vulnerability during maintenance work.
Command-remote tripping (attack) This requires penetration of external defenses. Unauthorized disconnection of circuits, potentially causing blackouts or grid instability.
Change in settings of relay (attack) An attacker alters the settings of relay for disabling the distance protection scheme. Increases the risk of system failure by preventing proper relay operation during faults.
Data injection (attack) Falsifying data by changing current, voltage, and sequence components for mimicking a fault and for misleading operators. Misleads operators, potentially causing blackouts and damaging equipment due to delayed response.

13.3 Methodology

In this manuscript, various ML classifiers are applied for IDS in power system. The CR, CM is developed for all the classifiers. Classifier performance is assessed based on ref. [10]:

  • CM: The CM is used to show how well classifiers are performing. By combining the actual classes with the predicted outcomes, it can display the specifics of the classifier’s classification outcome.

  • ROCC: It was proposed as a new criterion because validation accuracy cannot accurately represent a classifier’s true performance when the sample distribution is unbalanced. As shown in Figure 13.6, the Y-axis of the ROCC indicates the TPR, or sensitivity, and the X-axis shows the FPR.

  • Area Under Curve (AUC): In general, the classifier performs better the further it is from the ROCC to the Reference Line (a brown color line in Figure 13.6). Even while ROCC can intuitively represent a classifier’s performance, researchers always prefer to evaluate performance using a straightforward figure. Area under this ROCC is known as AUC. Thus, a high AUC value indicates a good classifier. 246.In this study, the effectiveness of several classifiers is assessed using these criteria [11].

9 Prone to overfitting Can be controlled using pruning techniques.
10 Foundation for ensemble methods Forms the basis of random forest, extra trees, and boosting algorithms.

13.6 Work on Xai: Application of Shap

  • Model 1 XGB: The Waterfall Plot:

The SHAP method is used for model’s predictions. The explanation of the first prediction is visualized using the command shap. plots. waterfall(shap_values[0]‌). The input provided to this plot is explanation object’s one row. Waterfall plot is intended 269.to show explanations for individual predictions. The expected Value (0.351 here) of the output of XGB is shown at the plot’s bottom part. Each row illustrates how each feature’s positive (red) or negative (blue) contribution shifts the value from the expected model output over the background dataset to the model output for this prediction. By default, SHAP uses the margin outputs of XGB Classifier to explain them before the logistic link function [23]. Thus, log-odds units are on the X-axis.

Waterfall Plot: This plot depicts the impact of various features on 50th instance. Every row in Figure 13.40 illustrates how the negative (blue) or positive (red) contribution of each feature alters the value from the anticipated output (E [f(x)= 0.351]) to the value predicted by the model (f (x)). Here, f(x) = E(f(x)) + SHAP value for each feature. The number next to each feature row reflects its associated observed value.

Each feature’s value for this sample is indicated by the gray text that appears before the feature names. When the feature numbers in the model surpasses the max display parameter, the features are arranged in the waterfall plot’s bottom part according to the SHAP magnitudes. Eighty-nine least significant features have been condensed into a single term in the explanation above. The max display argument can be used to alter the default limit of 10 rows. It is kept 40 in this plot. The command shap. plots.waterfall(shap_values = 50, max_display = 40) displays this plot for the 50th instance of the dataset. Red features are those that raise the prediction, while Blue features are those that lower it. Figure 13.40 shows this plot.

13.6.1 The Force Plot for Instance (50) for Label “0”

270.For looking the feature’s role in influencing the model’s prediction the “label” in a SHAP force plot refers to the predicted class or target value associated with the data point, while the “instance number” refers to the index of the data point chosen, essentially which row from the dataset is being explained [24]. The force plot illustrates how each feature affects the prediction for that particular data point. Every bar on 271.the plot denotes a feature, and the length of the bar shows how much of the prediction it contributed. The features that contributed to the “0” result are identified by looking at the first sample in the testing set. This will be accomplished by providing the SHAP, expected values and testing sample along with this force plot. The red bars typically show Positive_ Contributions, which push the prediction toward a greater value, and Blue bars show Negative_Contributions, which pull the prediction toward a lesser value.

Figure 13.41 shows the visualization of the 50th instance with a force plot using the command. This plot is created by selecting the instance number (50) and the corresponding label “0.”. The model output with index (0) is 0.95. After being converted into probability space, this “raw” value yields the final output of “0” and “1.” Figure 13.41 displays the base value as well as the features’ contributions to the “0” outcome. The mean of all the models’ output values during training is the base value. The contribution of Feature RP-M410: I = 632.6 is displayed in blue, while R2-PA5: IH = 162.4 is displayed in red. Other features’ contributions to label “0” for this instance are also displayed in Figure 13.41. The final output predicted by the model is “0” as the predicted value (0.95) is higher than (0).

13.6.2 The Force Plot for Instance (12) for label “1”

To determine which features contributed to the label “1,” the dataset’s 12th sample is selected. The force plot is used to enter the SHAP and expected values, and testing sample. Additionally, since the f(x) is 1.04 and greater than 1, it is observed that the model will belong to the “1” class or label. The base value and feature contributions to the “1” result are displayed in Figure 13.42. The contribution of feature R1-PA3: VH is –120.9, which is displayed in red, and the contribution of R3-PM2: V is 1.286e+5 in the last, which is displayed in blue. Other features’ contributions are also displayed. Y_test. iloc is the command used to test the prediction for 12th data point. The result is “1.” Figure 13.42 shows the force plot-2.

13.6.4 The Dependence Scatter Plot

The dependence scatter plot (DSP) is used for showing the effect of a single feature across the entire dataset. DSPs, as opposed to summary plots, illustrate the connection between a particular feature and the anticipated result for every data instance. Gaining more detailed information and checking the feature’s significance under study by supporting or refuting the outputs of the summary plots or other global feature importance metrics are just two of the many reasons this analysis is carried out. The X-axis shows the feature values to examine [25]. The SHAP value, for the model’s prediction for each data point, is displayed on the Y-axis. The various plots are displayed in Figures 13.48 to 13.51. The SHAP feature dependence plot shows interaction visualization. R1-PA1: VH interacts with R2-PM5: I. In values close to –150, the occurrence of an R2-PM5: I increases the value of R1-PA1: VH. Figures 13.50 and 13.51 show horizontal and vertical relationships.

13.6.5 The Scatter Plot

This plot uses the X-axis for plotting the feature’s value and its SHAP value on the Y-axis. This demonstrates how the model is reliant on the specified characteristic. The data points are used to represent the participants in this plot. This plot shows the Shap value for the variables in question placed against the underlying raw value. Different SHAP values can be produced from the same raw variable value because to interactions with other variables [26]. Figure 13.52 shows the horizontal relationship. Figure 13.53 shows the linearly increasing plot.

13.6.6 The Bee Swarm Plot

273.274.275.276.277.278.279.280.Each feature’s SHAP value for every sample is used for plotting. This is for providing a summary of the features that are most necessary for a model. Figure 13.54 employs SHAP values for depicting the distribution of each feature’s impact on the XGB’s 281.output. For all the samples, this graph organizes features according to the total of the magnitudes of the SHAP values. The feature’s values are represented by blue low, red high colors. The consequences of all the main characteristics are summed up in this plot. The ranking mean absolute SHAP values for all the variables in the dataset are shown on the Y-axis of the SHAP summary graph [27]. The command utilized for summarizing the impacts of all the features is shap. plots. beeswarm (shap_values).

13.6.7 The Global Bar Plot

The mean absolute value of the SHAP values for every feature is used to generate a standard bar plot. The command used is shap. plots. bar(shap_values). The plot is created by creating a SHAP values matrix and passing it to the bar plot function [28]. Figure 13.55 shows this plot and Figure 13.56 shows the stacked bar plot for binary-class outputs.

13.7 Work on Xai: Application of the Lime Method

To implement XAI using the LIME approach in Python, the LIME package is installed using the command! pip. The classification_report from sklearn.metrics, train test_split are imported. The data is split into a test dataset and a train dataset [32]. The training of the model is done using an ML model for making predictions on the testing dataset. The matplotlib.pyplot as plt is imported, and JS visualization code is loaded to the notebook as shap.initjs() . Using explainer = shap.TreeExplainer (clf) the explainer is created. It is required to import Shap, lime, lime_tabular, explanation class, and other required packages. The dataset is loaded. The coding is used for training an RF model on this OpenCV AI Ki (OAK) dataset by the use of RF classifier class from the ensemble module of sklearn. The coding is used for creating a LIME explainer instance with the help of lime_tabular module [33].

The subsequent step involves storing the output produced by the LIME explanation in an HTML file called op.html. The HTML file generated as output serves as the LIME explanation for the 50th instance in the OAK dataset. For the OAK dataset, the LIME explanation illustrates the contribution of each feature (P A1: V H – P A3: VH, etc.) to the predicted class (Natural, Attack) of the 50th instance. The outcome includes three primary pieces of information arranged from left to right.

  1. The predictions from the model
  2. The contributions from features300.
  3. 299. The real value for every feature

The following figures are generated using the RF classifier that displays a LIME result for the 50th instance and presents the final feature contribution in the form of table in orange and blue colors. It is observed that the 50th instance is predicted to have an attack with 100% confidence. Figures 13.83 to 13.91 show the results obtained from Python.

301.13.8 Conclusion and Future Work

Power system attacks and disturbances are the most frequent issues that regularly arise due to events caused by humans or nature. The biggest difficulty lies in identifying the primary reason for power disruption and taking suitable actions in response to it. Human judgment alone is not effective in forecasting power disturbances. It is a challenge to the operators to observe the system’s status. The objective of this research is to deploy various ML models and algorithms for identifying disturbances and dependably categorize them as either a natural or a harmful attack. The OAK dataset is used for implementing the ML algorithms with Python programming. The SG consists of a dual-layered framework: physical systems and cyber systems. The merging of the two systems establishes the cyber–physical setting. The PMU is operating in the digital component. It is used for providing the current information for managing the physical layer through energy control. The phasor data includes details regarding voltage and phasor measurements, including location of equipment like the switches, circuit breakers, transformers, and relays.

The SHAP and LIME methods from XAI are used for assessing the three models: ETC, RF and Light GBM. The highest values of the four metrics are obtained from the ETC model. The different visualization plots are shown for three models. A force plot, which is especially helpful for debugging model behavior or identifying areas where the model might be making incorrect predictions, is shown. The bee swarm plot is based on their individual SHAP values. Each participant of the dataset is represented by a dot on the bee swarm plot. When there is a large density of SHAP values, the dots are piled vertically. Each dot’s color represents the raw variable value of that person/feature. A high raw value is indicated by red, and a low raw value is shown by blue.

302.Future studies should deal with the real-time implementation of the proposed ML in the power system, integrating adaptive learning for evolving cyber-attack patterns. Expanding the dataset, incorporating DL, and fusing multi-source data can enhance accuracy. Further development of XAI will boost operator trust and decision-making in complex, high-risk cyber–physical scenarios.

315.14Artificial Intelligence (AI) GestureDraw: Hand Gesture-Based Drawing Interface with AI-Assisted Output Using Computer Vision and AI

Swathi Gowroju, Shilpa Choudhary, Annoji Sri Poojith, Puvvula Haritha, Shaga Preethika, and G. Sai Kiran

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-14

14.1 Introduction

In the past few decades, human–computer interaction (HCI) has changed dramatically from the traditional input devices of keyboards and mice to more natural and intuitive modalities such as touchscreens, voice commands, and hand gesture recognition. Of these, hand gesture recognition is one of the most transformative ways of allowing people to interact directly with digital systems. For instance, the initial motivation for gesture-based interfaces in the 1980s, in the “Videoplace” system developed by Myron Krueger, was fundamentally straightforward to make technology accessible and entertaining. Techniques have been advanced in computer vision and artificial intelligence, allowing very accurate and efficient recognition of gestures and bringing into reality innovative applications from gamification through to healthcare, education, and creative design. The existing works on hand gesture recognition are based on using different algorithms and technologies for the accurate interpretation of human gestures. For example, the traditional approach relies on edge detection and contour analysis as handcrafted features for the identification of gestures. Generally, all these methods were prone to failures because of variations caused by changes in lighting conditions, presence of background clutter, and inconsistent positioning or movement of hands, which adversely affected the accuracy of gesture recognition. 316.Due to deep learning, this discipline was revolutionized to let the machines learn even complex patterns from large datasets. So far, models such as convolutional neural network (CNN) and recurrent neural network (RNN) have been used in many gestures to achieve superior performance in different gesture recognition applications. Pre-trained models like MediaPipe Hands and OpenPose have continued to make hand detection and tracking in real time much easier using robust frameworks in gesture recognition applications.

Building on all the above developments, the proposed system, artificial intelligence (AI) GestureDraw, presents a novel hand gesture recognition that is combined with AI-driven output generation. While AI GestureDraw is unique in integrating real-time hand tracking coupled with advanced AI capabilities that go beyond interpretation for enhancing user-generated sketches as well as ensuring a seamless, intelligent user experience. In addition to letting users create digital sketches by tracing real-time hand gestures, this system uses AI to analyze and enhance the user’s sketches. As such, it essentially uses techniques in computer vision together with deep learning models to make sense of how hand movements will be translated to meaningful outputs. AI GestureDraw has several key elements that make up its innovative functionality:

  1. Hand Tracking and Gesture Recognition: (a) The system employs some state-of-the-art hand detection and tracking techniques that may identify the most important landmarks of the hand and interpret gestures with very high accuracy. (b) Algorithms such as CNNs may analyze spatial and temporal features of hand movements, and thus, the system will be able to distinguish which gesture stands for drawing, clearing the canvas, or invoking AI processing.
  2. Dynamic Content Generation: It has used artificial intelligence to interpret any sketch that is created, therefore providing context-related outputs. Such a process deals with interpreting a hand-drawn input and finding responses or solutions directly to that user’s intention.
  3. Interactive Interface: The system offers an intuitive and user-friendly platform for real-time interaction, where users can view their hand movements translated into drawings on the canvas while simultaneously receiving AI-generated feedback or solutions.

The proposed system transforms digital creativity and engagement via the use of artificial intelligence and computer vision. It dispenses with conventional input devices by deciphering natural hand motions, enabling users to create or sketch naturally. By improving forms, fixing mistakes, or offering original ideas instantly, AI improves this process. The applications are numerous and include rehabilitation, which provides accessible tools for people with motor impairments; creative arts and design, which enable complex creations; and education, which gives interactive learning experiences. Other applications include product design and prototyping, which streamlines idea generation; immersive virtual reality and augmented reality (VR/AR) experiences, which enable users to engage with three-dimensional (3D) places; gaming, which enables gesture-based interactions; and collaborative tools for 317.virtual meetings. This technology transforms by combining AI-driven improvements with simplicity. AI GestureDraw is a prime example of taking human instinct toward technological precision and its application in a methodical and integral manner. Combining gesture recognition capabilities at advanced levels with generative AI (GenAI), the system both simplifies processes in the creation and interaction with digital content but offers new scopes of innovation across domains. This paper provides insight into the technical foundation that supports AI GestureDraw, such as its development and underlying algorithms for the purpose of revolutionizing engagement in digital systems.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 14.2 includes the literature survey, and the proposed system is discussed in Section 14.3. Section 14.4 shows the result analysis and comparative analysis of the proposed system with state-of-the-art techniques. Sectiosn 14.5 concludes the proposed work.

14.2 Literature Survey

Hand gesture recognition is one of the developing domains in HCI with several breakthroughs designed to enhance precision, real-time execution, and usability of the applications, including touchless interfaces. A good portion of work performed in the above domain [1–12] differs in the applied techniques, such as CNNs, optical flow, and media-based hand tracking, and each technique offers a unique contribution toward accuracy and proficiency in gesture recognition. Despite that, the research regarding integrating gesture-based interaction with AI-powered feedback mechanisms remains very low, indicating more depth in this domain. Table 14.1 shows the survey of literature of AI-based hand gesture recognition.

Reddy et al. [1] and Khan et al. [5] have explored CNN-based hand gesture recognition models to significant benefits by providing 95.2% and 96.8% accuracy rates, respectively. Though the methods work fairly well with isolated gesture recognition, the actual implementation of such systems in interactive real-time systems usually appears to suffer from challenges faced in uncontrolled lighting conditions and complex environments. Other related researchers come forward and have proposed hand detection with the solution of MediaPipe and YOLO proposed by Yusuf et al. [2] and Podder et al. [3], respectively, which are able to solve some of the discussed issues mentioned above, particularly in dynamic settings, but for real-time tracking, there is still much room for improvement.

Recently, significant interest has developed in systems that recognize gestures and facilitate communication in creative fields, drawing, or educational tools. Few really depend on the camera positions. Researchers [4, 7] have explored deep learning techniques along with traditional computer vision algorithms, for example, Haar Cascade features and Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) features. However, the accuracy of those methods, while being efficient, remains suboptimal compared with much more sophisticated models, specifically CNN and long short-term memory (LSTM)-based models [6]. Other approaches are based on machine learning and techniques of optical flow as proposed by Alonazi et al. [8] and Rastgoo et al. [7], which have also been found promising toward gesture recognition with potential applicability in gesture-based user interfaces, but point to difficulties in the accuracy 318.of tracking when gestures are too fast or ambiguous. Lastly, several research studies recently have actually pointed out context-aware recognition systems, especially AI-based feedback, as cited by Ansar et al. [10]. These are actually designed to be even more adaptive in responses, depending on hand movement and combinations of gestures toward intelligent applications that are gesture-driven. Despite this, it is evident that the effort to design systems more robust and flexible with a view toward accepting a variety of hand postures and real-time situations will remain an important objective of this future research.

319.14.3 Proposed Work

The introduction of new ideas to increase user interaction and creativity with innovative hand gesture recognition and artificial intelligence is done in the current paper [13]. AI GestureDraw is developed based on the strong foundation of techniques related to computer vision and deep learning. The proposed system will allow people to create an interactive way of making drawings with hand gestures, thus possibly accelerating the process of drawing and elevating it by AI-assisted output generation [14]. At the end of completing a sketch, the system intelligently analyzes the drawing and gives task-specific responses for it to be a versatile tool for various applications[15]. AI GestureDraw allows for smooth, engaging user experience while encouraging creativity, harnessing the power of analytics through AI, in giving meaning to sketches in real time [16]. The methodology proposed for this application involves capturing video input live through a webcam, identifying user hand gestures as illustrated in Figure 14.1 to interpret their drawings, and generating meaningful outputs according to the drawings input [17].

The system architecture shown in Figure 14.1 describes how the proposed model works. First, the video input is given which is through the camera; it captures live video of the user. The camera first detects the user’s hand and then finds out all the sensor marks out of our hand deciding on identification of the fingers. The purpose of all these functions will be to identify face(s) in a live video input—a constant stream of data to be processed. This input is divided into frames, where each frame offers a glimpse of the video [18]. These frames are subsequently transformed into grayscale images, discarding color data that does not contribute to recognizing the structure. The most important element to classify is the gesture. This is then followed by a pre-processing step where things like noise reduction, normalization, and contrast enhancement can be performed to make the frames ready for further analysis. This makes sure raw input data appears consistent and clean so the model can accurately detect and classify images.

This process will consist of a series of steps:

  • Data Collection: The initial step would be the collection of various datasets of hand gestures and drawings. This dataset contains a variety of hand movements and sketch examples from different users, which would serve as a basis for training the gesture recognition model.
  • Gesture Recognition: The system will apply computer vision techniques for the live feeds from the webcam to analyze it. It implements a pre-trained model like Mediapipe to detect accurate hand gestures that represent the drawing actions with strokes, shapes, and symbols. Such recognition by gestures ensures accurate interpretation of the user’s intentions.
  • Input Capture: Once the user completes their drawing, user can halt the live feed of the video using some specific gesture, as shown in Figure 14.2. This will capture the input so drawn, and then the system will freeze the video and proceed to perform the concerned sketch for further processing.
  • AI Output Generation: The system captures the input as a sketch and sends it to a model of AI, which evaluates the content (using the gesture from 320.321.Figure 14.2f). Here, the AI uses the deep learning techniques to comprehend the drawing and produces relevant output depending on the intent of the user-to solve a problem, answer a question, or give feedback.
  • Presenting the Output to the User: The outcomes thus produced are presented in an easy-to-follow accessible style where the user can easily interact with the results. This could be through text, visual enhancements, or other active elements that encourage user-friendliness of the system.

The system introduces a strong mechanism of feedback which allows users to alter the illustration or input it produces based on the AI output. In this way, the process generates creativity and gives results that meet the expectations with the closest results possible. This harmonious HCI generates an overall enriched user experience where the outputs align with the user’s vision.

After pre-processing, the hand detector runs on each frame to check for the presence of a hand as shown in Figure 14.2. The system loops back to continue checking the video feed if no hand is detected. Upon detection of a hand, the system proceeds to gesture recognition stage which employs a deep learning model based on MobileNetV2. It is also a full CNN with 53 layers, perfect for real-time applications, building efficiency and accuracy. Using the pre-trained models under cvzonelike, MobileNetV2 analyzes the hand data to recognize specific gestures according to predefined patterns. However, data is ongoing to learn the recognized gestures by the system, so the system can know and reciprocate them accordingly.

Figure 14.2 shows how a computer vision-based AI interface that uses hand gestures operates. Landmark identification of the hand is demonstrated in the first phases (Figure 14.2a–d), where nodes stand in for joints or fingers and connecting lines, most likely produced by pose estimate techniques, create the hand structure. Active gesture detection is demonstrated in stage (Figure 14.2e), which shows the raw video stream with the user’s hand identified and tracked using a bounding box. In the last step (Figure 14.2f–h), the interface is displayed where the system decodes gestures like “number 1” or a “fist,” and produces AI-assisted outputs marked “Answer.” This demonstrates the smooth transition from hand recognition to gesture interpretation, opening the door for uses such as sign language translation, virtual sketching, and gesture-based control systems.

The gesture recognition module is capable of recognizing multiple commands. For example, when detecting only the index finger, the system is able to “draw,” but recognizing all five fingers closed would delete the previous drawing. Zooming operates with gestures similar to index and thumb fingers together, and all fingers except the thumb represent a video freeze operation. Once the gesture has been processed, an AI-based output is generated depending on the detected gesture. This textual output yields an output (like drawing a space or freezing a block) or a summarization of the system response. This multi-layered structure enables the seamless integration of live gesture recognition, action execution, and feedback, and is suitable for applications such as virtual drawing boards, gesture-controlled presentations, or smart environments. All the components work together to provide a seamless and immersive user interface.

322.323.14.3.1 Training

The model is intended for tasks involving feature extraction and classification. It starts with two 16-filter convolutional layers (Conv2D). While the second convolutional layer shrinks the spatial dimensions to (22, 22, 16), the first convolutional layer generates an output of size (48, 48, 16).

Batch normalization comes after these layers, normalizing the feature maps to speed up and stabilize the training process. The model has two MaxPooling2D layers that downsample the feature maps to (24, 24, 16) and (11, 11, 16) correspondingly to further minimize the spatial dimensions and avoid overfitting. To enhance the model’s capacity for generalization, Dropout layers are also used following each pooling operation, randomly removing a portion of neurons during training. The graphs illustrated in Figure 14.2 show how well a model performs throughout training and validation across several epochs. The training and validation accuracy progression is displayed in the accuracy graph. The model is successfully learning from the training data when the training accuracy (blue line) rises gradually across epochs and approaches 1.0. In a similar vein, the validation accuracy (orange line) achieves excellent accuracy with very slight variations. The model appears to generalize effectively to unknown data without experiencing severe overfitting, as indicated by the tight alignment between training and validation accuracy.

The loss and accuracy graphs are shown in Figure 14.3. It shows that plots for training and validation loss are decreased over the same time periods. The model’s predictions on the training data are getting increasingly accurate as the training loss (blue line) drops off dramatically in the first few epochs and then gradually till it approaches zero. Comparable to the training loss, the validation loss (orange line) 324.shows a similar pattern, sharply decreasing and leveling out at a low number. For training and validation data, the model performs admirably overall, demonstrating high accuracy and minimal loss. Effective learning and superior generalization to unknown data are highlighted by the strong correlation between the training and validation parameters. This result shows that the dataset, model architecture, and hyperparameters are all set up for the job.

14.3.2 Evaluation Parameters

The proposed system uses gesture recognition accuracy (GRA), latency (L), and AI output relevance (OR) to ensure the performance of the proposed system. GRA is calculated using Equation 14.1, which helps to identify the total number of correct gestures out of total number of gestures performed.

GRA = (T_correct/T_total) × 100% (14.1)

where T_correct is the number of correctly recognized gestures, and T_total is the total gestures tested. L is calculated using Equation 14.2, which helps to identify the approximate time to identify the gestures that are being performed.


$$\text{L} = \frac{\left( {\sum_{\text{i} = 1}^{\text{n}}\text{T}\_\text{recognize},\text{i}} \right)}{}\text{n}$$
 (14.2)

where T_recognize, i is the Time taken to recognize gesture I. n is the number of gestures tested. OR is calculated using Equation 14.3, which helps to identify the number of relevant AI outputs out of the total number of outputs received.

OR = (S_relevant / S_total) × 100 % (14.3)

where S_relevant is the number of AI outputs deemed relevant by evaluators, S_total is the total outputs evaluated.

14.4 RESULTS

The proposed system uses advanced gesture recognition technology, combined with GenAI, to ensure a responsive and interactive experience. Incorporating computer vision, hand tracking, and AI-powered capabilities, this system provides gesture-based interactions in real-time designed for creative, educational, and problem-solving applications. It provides an integrated platform for users to visualize concepts, execute actions, and get contextual AI-generated answers. The results of the proposed system show the operation and output of the AI-powered hand gesture detection and interactive app. Utilizing computer vision, hand tracking, and generative AI, this system examines users in real-time and enables an interactive experience driven by gestures. This application utilizes powerful libraries, including OpenCV and cvzone 325.for gesture detection, as well as Google’s GenAI for generating responses, thereby creating a real-time interface where users can visualize their imaginations and interact using gesture-based actions to get AI-generated responses. The entire system is initiated with a real-time webcam input where cvzone HandTrackingModule fetches and analyzes hand gestures. Upon the user’s index finger, the system receives this gesture, and the tracking of its movement starts. Then the user can draw freehand on the virtual canvas (as shown in Figure 14.4). Drawing is fluid and responsive, simulating the experience of drawing directly against the surface while also having the accuracy to track the finger’s path.

  • Clear Canvas Gesture: When the user lifts only the thumb, this action is interpreted as a request to clear the entire canvas. This resets the workspace so the user is left with new processes and no requirement to input data or engage in complex interactions.

  • Interpretation Based on AI: Four fingers up (as shown in Figure 14.3) summon the links with GenAI from Google. It stores the user’s drawing as an image and runs it through the AI model to produce a contextualized response. For example, if a mathematical problem is sketched on the canvas, the AI can provide a solution as a text output (as shown in Figure 14.5). This feature exemplifies how AI can deepen user engagement, including interpreting visual input and yielding 326.meaningful results. By overlaying the webcam feed with the actual virtual canvas, this system provides real-time visualization as well as feedback to the users. Moreover, the text output generated by any AI is presented in the user interface dynamically, providing instantaneous feedback and interaction.

This is a real-time gesture-based learning application powered by an AI system and is both easy to use and can be used for multiple purposes. With cvzone’s ability to track the hand accurately and the integration of GenAI responses, this component creates an interactive and engaging experience. We highlight here the system’s ability to integrate computational and creative tasks through the drawing and AI-based content generation functionalities.

The system’s accuracy, responsiveness, and real-time feedback efficiency are exemplary. The hand tracking is powerful with low latency and the correct recognition of gestures, in the same light conditions. Basically, drawing devices have some AI-supported functions. The canvas responds to gestures with intuitive commands, and the system is accessible to users of all skill levels as the actions feel incredibly natural and flexible on the canvas.

For practical applications, virtual whiteboarding, teaching aids, and creative tools also hold great promise with this application. Through its ability to interpret rich inputs and produce automated outputs, the AI-driven feature expands the utility of the system by serving as a bridge between user creativity and machine intelligence. Maximize info (with fewer words) “In all, these results show the applicability of computer vision, gesture recognition, and AI-based processing into a live, real-time interactive system.” It uses LF-based system. Table 14.2 shows the performance metrics of the proposed system.

Table 14.2 Evaluation Metrics of Proposed System⏎
MetricUsed Achieved Accuracy Comment

The system is showing excellent performance and efficiency across some metrics, areas, indicating the success of the proposal for making gesture recognition or AI-assisted tasks which are working on gesture to work efficiently. Results were measured in terms of GRA, which reached an impressive 96.2% on a custom dataset 327.of 15 dynamic gestures, thus demonstrating the reliability of the system in accurately interpreting user inputs. The average latency (L) was 82 ms per gesture, proving their system can return near-real-time responses, important for interactive applications. Furthermore, AI OR reached 94.5%, indicative of the ability of the system to offer relevant outputs in INCOTERMS, throughout educational, creative, and problem-solving situations. Together, these metrics demonstrate the reliability, versatility, and applicability of the proposed system as a potential candidate for gesture-based and AI solutions.

14.4.1 Comparative Analysis

One of the major advantages of the proposed system is its real-time gesture-based drawing functionality. In contrast to most of the systems presently available [1], the proposed system allows the HCI in real time by directly raising the index finger to engage in the dynamic process of direct drawing. Most of the other systems present today focus on static gesture recognition and some classify previously defined hand movements. This capability brings in a more interactive and engaging environment for the system, making it more flexible and user-friendly. In contrast, traditional systems are limited to only detecting and interpreting gestures without enabling direct manipulation of the drawing or visual output.

The inclusion of AI into the proposed system introduces an important feature that may largely be missing in most of the existing systems. However, once the user has produced his or her drawing, the system transfers the captured image to an AI model for processing the produced drawing and generating context-specific outputs. This might be solving a particular problem, giving long detailed explanations, or creating creative content based on the entered input. Currently, however, such systems as those based on CNNs or support vector machines (SVMs) only indicate that gestures can be recognized and classified and do not present any additional output or interaction. This proposed system will be full of many capabilities due to the AI nature, but these are expanded functionalities that make it capable for more rigorous applications-educational tools, creative platforms, and AI-driven design.

328.The key idea behind this proposed system is its capability to map a variety of actions onto a number of gestures. For instance, one could draw with one gesture and erase with another. This gesture control, driven by a more refined user experience compared with the current systems limited to only recognizing predefined static gestures without providing the capacity to carry out complex tasks, is another promising development. For example, one can clear the canvas using a simple thumb gesture or even initiate a new drawing using another gesture. This dynamic control over the actions executed by the system makes it very efficient for creative tasks and has a positive advantage over other existing gesture recognition systems, which do not have multi-action capabilities.

Although the proposed application has higher diversity and application than the existing systems, mainly used for the recognition of simple gestures or classification in HCI and sign language interpretation, the system’s capabilities only extend into more diverse practical applications. Combining the gesture recognition aspect with that of AI, the system becomes very suitable for use in interactive drawing tools, digital art creations, education settings, and virtual whiteboards. The capability to solve problems, such as mathematical equations or even diagrams drawn by a user, is also integrated into AI. This extension of the scope of application definitely highlights the flexibility of the proposed system while providing the end-users with a more complete tool compared to the clearer definitions, yet simpler system types derived from the literature study.

14.4.2 Positive Aspects

It lets users draw and touch a virtual canvas in real time using hand gestures, creating a dynamic, immersive experience compared to most static gesture recognition systems. With AI processing integrated to process the drawn input, beyond gesture recognition, the system is enabled to be more intelligent and far more versatile when users can get context-specific outputs. It gives the user an added advantage with control and flexibility through support that can be drawn, erased, or stopped to maximize the efficiency of the tool for creative and productive purposes. The very integration of gesture recognition and AI combines manifold applications, from virtual whiteboards to digital art, educational platforms, to problem-solving tools.

Most of them adopted different algorithms and techniques along with different datasets that helped overcome these problems with detecting and classifying gestures correctly. Zhang and Lu [19] used a CNN for gesture recognition but added Kalman filtering with accuracy at 95.2%. Similar work also involves Gupta et al. [20]. It used a CNN-based deep learning approach that exhibited high accuracy up to 96.8% on the Hand Gesture Recognition Database (HGRD). Bhiri et al. [21] used MediaPipe for the detection of hand landmarks and K-nearest neighbors (KNNs) for gesture classification. Patel et al. [22] adopted OpenPose for hand key point detection coupled with a Random Forest classifier, with both systems achieving remarkable accuracy: 92.7% and 91.0%, respectively.

329.Although these existing systems, as shown in Figure 14.4, have very high recognition accuracy, they focus mostly on gesture detection and classification, with very minimal interactivity and feedback. Approaches like those from Lee et al. [23], which use YOLO for hand detection, and Kim et al. [24] using Haar Cascade Classifiers, have shown high levels of performance in gesture recognition but do not offer real-time, context-aware responses based on the recognized gestures.

The proposed system offers a novel addition by presenting the integration of real-time GenAI responses together with gesture recognition. Compared to existing approaches, the system under discussion differs significantly in the respect that the approach has made its primary emphasis on the integration of the model of a GenAI so as to dynamically and in accordance with contexts produce feedback given by recognized gestures. This AI-powered interaction enables the system to accomplish tasks such as mathematical problem-solving, answering questions, or giving appropriate information based on user gestures. This interactivity layer is of significant value and makes the experience of the user much more personal and responsive in nature. Unlike existing systems, the proposed system offers a more versatile solution that can adapt to various user needs because it is not limited to gesture detection and classification. The system utilizes Streamlit for the user interface to ensure smooth and efficient real-time processing, and the GenAI model makes it intuitive and seamless for users. By combining gesture recognition with AI-powered feedback, the proposed system represents a significant advancement in the field, providing a more comprehensive solution for applications such as HCI, virtual assistants, and sign language translation, setting it apart from traditional models that focus exclusively on gesture detection or classification without offering meaningful post-gesture actions.

330.The video feed system also provides another form of benefit through hand gesture control, where specific movements in the hand, including lifting all fingers, send a signal to freeze the real-time feed with that particular content to be captured, meaning that there is a certain intuitive and accuracy attribute of control as the person controlling the drawing process does not have to stretch out to touch some form of remote control. This functionality is not possible in existing systems because they are mainly designed for classifying gestures from continuous video feeds. The pause and resume support of video feeds through gestures makes the overall system much more interactive in nature and gives the user maximum flexibility to capture content at the right moment.

14.5 Conclusion and Future Scope

In this proposed system, we developed an interactive hand gesture recognition application using the latest computer vision techniques and machine learning algorithms to allow real-time user interaction. The system consists of several functional modules, such as hand and finger detection algorithms (using techniques like CNNs and Haar Cascades) to precisely locate hand landmarks and follow their movements in videos or images. Using KNNs, SVM, decision tree and machine learning algorithms were used for gesture recognition, where classification is done based on the relative position of fingers and hand movements to recognize the gestures. Integrating these methodologies allows the program to interactively react to user inputs, allowing for actions in real-time such as sketching on a canvas or potentially erasing it from specific gestures. The key to detection and classification accuracy during implementation is to preprocess the input data, such as by minimizing noise in the audio and making sure that all frames are processed in the same manner. These results also proved the advantage of starting with a clean and responsive canvas to improve the user experience and provided a clear demonstration of the system’s ability to provide an accurate and reliable gesture-based method of interaction.

Although the proposed system managed to include vital features such as drawing and clearing the canvas by gestures, there are several opportunities for improvement in the future. One exciting direction includes exploiting state-of-the-art machine learning methods like deep learning models. For example, using CNNs for more efficient feature extraction or using RNNs for processed gesture data could improve the accuracy of recognition greatly. Furthermore, integrating handwriting analysis techniques, particularly optical character recognition (OCR) or CNN models for character recognition, would broaden the system’s applications in areas like digital handwriting recognition and signature verification. For further development, we can even use different kinds of algorithms like Naive Bayes Classifier or LSTM networks, as we could even do a sentiment analysis of users based on the gesture. Furthermore, extending the system to accommodate a wider selection of gestures as well as allowing greater interactivity in real time would further develop the application. In the fast-evolving field of user interface design, the proposed system could keep pace with technological advancements and changing user requirements.
