333.15Improved Fetal Electrocardiogram Detection Using a Hybrid Wavelet-Based Denoising Method

K. Naga Sankar Reedy, Peddapullaiahgari Hariobulesu, Shaik Karimullah, Anwar Bhasha Pattan, Fahimuddin Shaik, and Mudassir Khan

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-15

15.1 Introduction

There are two main ways to measure fetal electrocardiogram (fECG): aggressive and non-invasive. Non-invasive abdominal electrocardiogram (ECG) records a signal that includes both the mother’s and the baby’s heartbeats. Invasive methods, on the other hand, entail putting electrodes unswervingly on the baby’s scalp once the cervix has opened during delivery [1]. You can start monitoring a baby’s heart rate without surgery as early as the first trimester by putting electrodes on the mother’s stomach. However, noise from power cables, skin-electrode impedance, and the mother’s muscular activity can often hamper the working of this method [2]. It is very important to look at the fECG to check the health of the baby’s heart and find problems such as congenital cardiac abnormalities, bradycardia, tachycardia, and hypoxia [3]. There are various ways to extract fECG data, namely linear decomposition, adaptive filtering, and nonlinear transformation [4]. A linear method like single-value decomposition (SVD) will provide additive segregated sources in terms of both their temporal and spectral characteristics that are based on a base function that may be predetermined or data-driven [5]. A blind source separation (BSS) method, such as independent component analysis (ICA) and its variants, assumes the signal source matrices are statistically independent. The more recent concept of periodic component analysis (πCA) has been demonstrated as a semi-blind separation method when working with or without a priori knowledge [6]. A situation in which fECG data is contaminated with extensive noise requires non-linear methods, such as using delayed copies of the disturbed 334.signal to approximately recover its state space, and thus properly filtering the signal by still using a method like principal component analysis (PCA) or similar [7]. These types of methods do work quite well with noticeable improvements in accuracy, but are computationally intensive and can be contingent on subjective bounds determined by expert opinion [8]. Adaptive filtering is still used frequently today, but it typically requires an ECG signal reference from the maternal fetus and would also certainly require committed signal channels from the maternal ECG (mECG) if it is independent [9]. In the absence of an ECG reference source, fECG can be computed using successive cancellation methods, although there will not necessarily be any satisfactory performance in eliminating all mECG activity (Figure 15.1). There are also variants proposed based on wavelet transform (WT)-based methods that have been proven to perform satisfactorily too, especially when adaptive thresholding is applied to the wavelet coefficients. Extended Kalman smoothers are capable of extracting fECG from single-channel data, but they struggle when maternal and fetal signals blend. In summary, fetal ECG extraction from abdominal recordings is difficult due to overlapping signals and outside noise [10]. Complex signal processing techniques are necessary to enhance the quality and diagnostics of signals.

There are many approaches for fECG extraction. Kalman filter (KF) is becoming a valid solution to reduce noise in adaptive filtering. It has been recommended that an extended state KF could be used to extract fECG data after mixed abdominal signals. This method is more effective than standard Kalman filtering approaches. Recently, researchers have studied various approaches used to extract single-channel fECG, using qualitative and quantitative measures. One of these studies presents a new method of adaptive filtering to detect fetal QRS complexes in the maternal abdomen ECG signals. In addition, there is a proposed adaptive noise remover that incorporates many sub-filters to deliver a better fECG. The research is substantial, 335.and the techniques point toward a hybrid system of utilizing different techniques for estimating fetal heart rate (FHR). However, fECG signals are often concealed from the noise and artifacts of the abdominal signals and the fetal R-peak is not accurately discovered. In these moments, the stationary wavelet transform (SWT) is important because it is able to analyze non-stationary signals with frequency components that are continually changing. SWT is a useful method for extracting fECG because it may break down complicated abdominal signals. This is especially useful for monitoring and diagnosing abnormalities that happen before birth.

15.2 LITERATURE REVIEW

Camps et al. [11] suggested a way to get fECG data using a finite impulse response (FIR) neural network combined with a framework for adaptive noise reduction. This method worked better than typical least mean squares (LMS) and normalized least mean squares (NLMS) algorithms because it used nonlinear dynamic characteristics. It was able to extract fECG from both simulated and actual datasets. Sameni and Clifford [12] wrote a thorough assessment of the problems and future possibilities in fECG signal processing. They pointed out important obstacles, such as small signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), the lack of standardized benchmark databases, and the fact that we do not know much about how baby hearts work. The study also looked at how acquisition and signal dispensation techniques have improved over the past 40 years. Kanjilal et al. [13] came up with a way to extract a single-channel fECG by means of SVD. They showed that this method works well for separating maternal and fetal signals at a reasonable computational cost. Al-Zaben and Al-Smadi [14] built on this by creating a hybrid method that used SVD and a neuro-fuzzy reasoning system to adaptively cancel noise. Their solution combined reference signals produced from SVD and fuzzy logic to improve filtering. It worked very well on equally synthetic and real-world fECG data.

15.3 EXISTING METHOD

There has to be a way to correctly find fetal heartbeats so that fetal heart health can be monitored during early pregnancy. This paper suggests two hybrid algorithms for extracting fECG data using the recursive least squares (RLS) approach. Finding the fetal R-peaks accurately is very important for diagnosing and treating congenital cardiac problems. The main goal is to separate the fECG signal from the combined abdominal recording. RLS is a commonly used method in adaptive signal processing to reduce noise and separate signals [15]. The RLS algorithm works by continuously estimating the mECG and then subtracting the mECG estimated from the abdominal signal, in a time-varying manner, and letting the fECG in the remaining error be more easily viewable. The RLS algorithm will continually adjust the filter coefficients for different time instances of the input signal to ensure that the difference between the input signal and the reference signal is as small as possible. Some of the extraction components of RLS are filter settings, residual error calculations, filter weight adjustments, and Kalman gain calculations. RLS is ideal for real-time applications as it continually optimizes the filter as the estimate is intended to be closer to the signal 336.the measurement of interest. These points make RLS a powerful method for differentiating fECG from mECG and ambient noise.

15.3.1 Signal Preprocessing

  • Band-Pass Filtering: Apply a band-pass filter to the raw abdominal ECG signal to isolate the frequency range of the ECG (e.g., 0.5–50 Hz) and remove high-frequency noise and baseline wander.
  • Segmentation: Break down the signal into smaller segments if needed for processing efficiency.

15.3.2 RLS Filter Setup

  • The RLS filter adapts to minimize the error e(k)e(k)e(k) between a reference input (mECG) and the abdominal ECG (mixed mECG and fECG).

15.3.3 Key Components

  • Reference Signal: A clean mECG obtained from chest electrodes serves as the reference signal.
  • Primary Signal: The abdominal ECG, which contains both mECG and fECG.
  • Filter Coefficients: The weights w(k), which are iteratively updated.

15.3.4 Filter Equations

  • Prediction Error:
e(k) = d(k) − WTx(k) (15.1)
  • where d(k) is the desired signal, x(k) is the input vector (reference signal), and w(k) is the weight vector.
  • Kalman Gain:
$\text{K}\left( \text{k} \right) = \frac{\text{P}\left( {\text{k} - 1} \right)\text{x}\left( \text{k} \right)}{\lambda + \text{X}^{\text{T}}\left( \text{k} \right)\text{P}\left( {\text{k} - 1} \right)\text{x}\left( \text{k} \right)}$ (15.2)
  • where P is the inverse correlation matrix, and λ is the forgetting factor (close to 1 for slower adaptation).
  • Filter Update:
w(k) = w(k−1) + K(k)e(k) (15.3)
  • Covariance Update:
$P\left( k \right) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\left\lbrack {P\left( {k - 1} \right) - K\left( k \right)X^{T}\left( k \right)P\left( {k - 1} \right)} \right\rbrack$ (15.4)

337.15.3.5 mECG Cancellation

  • Apply the RLS filter to adaptively subtract the mECG (as modeled by the reference) from the abdominal ECG.
  • The output e(k)e(k)e(k) is primarily the fECG with residual noise.

15.3.6 Post-Processing

  • Apply additional filtering or noise reduction techniques to enhance the fECG signal.
  • Techniques such as wavelet denoising or ICA can further improve signal quality.

15.4 PROPOSED METHOD

To reliably assess fetal cardiac activity during early pregnancy, an elaborate method is required to detect fetal heartbeats. In this paper, we will provide two methods to recover fECG using a combination of the SWT and RLS algorithm. In the wavelet domain, we will use either a threshold-based denoising technique or an improved spatially selective noise filtering (ISSNF) method to enhance the fECG signal, remove noise and artifacts, and accurately find R-peaks. Accurate identification of R-peaks is relevant to early diagnosis and treatment of fetal heart abnormalities while providing doctors with valuable evolving data about the state of the fetus. A major aim is to produce an obvious articulatory fECG from a very disorganized stomach ECG. The proposed method begins with separating the abdominal signal into multiscale components using an SWT. The scale of decomposition can be adjusted according to the noise content. The RLS algorithm is used to suppress the mother’s ECG components of the fECG before utilizing either the threshold-based technique or the ISSNF filtering approach to suppress the noise. We used our method on synthetic and real datasets. We used qualitative and quantitative metrics, such as visually inspecting the data, identifying the QRS complex, and calculating the SNR, to evaluate performance. The results of the experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional adaptive filtering methods, and the resulting SNR is consistent, with significantly less interference and accurate extraction of clean fECG data (Figure 15.2).

WT is a powerful tool for processing biological signals and has been widely used in applications such as noise removal from the ECG signal. The WT does not have any restrictions and is capable of processing non-stationary and time-varying signals, making it particularly useful for fECG data analysis. Wavelet processing allows for more flexible multiresolution analysis, which enables analysis of the low-frequency trend of the signal, as well as the higher frequency components of the signal. This is necessary for fECG extraction, as fetal heart signals can generally be lost inside the mECG signals and other noise sources. Furthermore, as WT may transition through multiple frequency bands, it provides a greater capacity for the separation of fetal heart activity also. The use of SWT is applied here, as it provides a stable time-frequency representation which is particularly helpful when seeking the dynamic features of the 338.fECG signal, specifically locating the R-peaks in the fECG signal accurately. The wavelet domain is also a potential pathway for filtering noise ultimately by capitalizing on the positive features of the fECG signal sparsity and energy concentration features. We reconstruct the extraction process using the RLS method in the wavelet domain, which provides a useful capability to remove the noise and interference contributed by the mother while retaining important fetal heart properties.

15.4.1 ISSNF Technique

To extract the fECG accurately, it is necessary to develop an effective denoising strategy based on wavelet analysis, and one of the derived methods, the spatially selective noise filter (SSNF), is a robust way to analyze biological signals and processes (Figure 15.3). The SSNF can effectively remove noise without losing the original signal of fECG, including the signal features resulting from the waveform shape, amplitude, and frequency content. The SSNF’s approach allows for the removal of undesired components without altering the fECG signal. Importantly, the SSNF can reject multiple sources of interference, including but not limited to, baseline drift, powerline noise, and noise from electromyographic signals. The fECG signal can provide diagnostic clarity after removal of most, if not all, the noise.

339.The ISSNF method is an improved version of the conventional SSNF used to improve SNR performance. This method is based on finding the spatial correlation, CorR(g, k), in distinct parts of the signal at each wavelet scale g. The idea behind this method is that the components of the signal are more physically linked in space whereas the components of noise are weakly correlated or not correlated. ISSNF exploits the difference to favor retention of more important structures of the signal while removing uncorrelated noise. This will help make the meaning of the signal more apparent and ensure the best possible fECG readings are obtained.

15.4.2 Threshold-Based Algorithm

Both hard and soft thresholding are common methods used to remove noise in the wavelet domain. While soft thresholding is generally very good at smoothly shrinking wavelet coefficients, hard thresholding has even been shown to have better results in some cases, particularly when the focus is on preserving sharp features in the signal. Research has shown that hard thresholding operates quite well with the undecimated wavelet transform (UWT) or the SWT. This is because hard thresholding is capable of preserving important signal patterns over all scales. In this case, a simple, but effective hard thresholding algorithm is described. This algorithm is a simple way of achieving signal de-noising while preserving the structure of the fECG signal.

15.4.3 Method for fECG Extraction

This research examines two hybrid approaches to extract fECG signals, as the abdominal ECG signals are complex and changing. The proposed methods offer two different processing pathways, which would allow an overall assessment and comparison of the outputs between the two methods. In Method 1, the RLS algorithm, the 340.SWT, and the ISSNF were employed. Method 2 is similarly arranged, but instead of ISSNF, it uses a threshold-based denoising approach.

There are four main steps in each method:

  • Using SWT for multi-resolution decomposition
  • RLS-based adaptive filtering to cancel out the mother’s ECG,
  • Using either ISSNF (Method 1) or thresholding (Method 2) to get rid of noise,
  • Measuring and analyzing fECG.

The SWT breaks down both abdominal and thoracic signals into several degrees of resolution. We have assessed the reconstruction performance of different wavelets as selected from the MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox. The performance of the reconstruction of Bior 1.5 was selected, as it had the best quality of reconstruction. A level of decomposition of five is chosen due to the nature of the signal’s frequency characteristics. Adaptive RLS filtering is then performed on the approximation and detailed coefficients in the wavelet domain. The abdomen coefficients will be considered the primary input, and the thorax coefficients will be considered the reference input. This adaptive filtering technique will effectively start to isolate and remove the mECG process while still prioritizing the fECG process above the remaining signals. There can still be artifacts or noise present in the recovered signals. Method 1 uses the ISSNF algorithm to selectively eliminate noise. This algorithm assumes that signal components are strongly correlated in space while noise components are weakly correlated. Method 2, on the other hand, uses a rigorous thresholding method to get rid of noise while keeping important parts of the fECG. For each wavelet scale, spatial correlations are calculated for both the approximation and detail coefficients to help with the denoising process. We evaluate the findings from both methods to see how well they keep the signal’s integrity and make the fECG clearer.

15.5 RESULTS

Figure 15.4 shows the steps in Method 1 for fECG extraction that require processing the signals. The top plot shows the raw abdominal signal, which is a combination of the mother’s ECG, the baby’s ECG, and other noise signals. The main peaks in this signal are mostly caused by the mother’s heart beating, which can hide the smaller parts of the fECG. The middle plot displays the thoracic signal taken from the mother’s chest. Most of it is a clean mECG. This reference signal is very important for adaptive filtering, especially the RLS algorithm, because it lets us accurately estimate and subtract the mECG from the abdominal signal. The bottom figure shows the final fECG that was retrieved after using signal processing methods such as the ISSNF algorithm, the SWT, and inverse wavelet reconstruction. The resulting waveform clearly shows fetal heart activity, with a lot of noise and maternal artifacts being removed. These results show that Method 1 works to separate fECG signals from complicated recordings of the abdomen.

Figure 15.5 shows how to find the R-peak in the fECG signal that was taken using Method 1. The blue waveform shows the final fECG signal that was left after taking 341.out the mother’s ECG parts and noise artifacts. There are red markers on top of this signal that show where the identified R-peaks are. These are the most conspicuous and quick upward deflections in each cardiac cycle. Finding these R-peaks correctly is very important for figuring out the FHR and checking on the baby’s health during pregnancy. The successful detection of R-peaks shows that the extraction approach works and that the important morphological features of the fECG have been kept. In addition, being able to accurately identify R-peaks provides a way to check that the whole signal processing pipeline is strong and accurate. These results prove that Method 1 can reliably separate the fECG from the rest of the data while keeping the diagnostic features needed for clinical evaluation.

Figure 15.6 shows the outcomes of Method 2’s signal processing pipeline for extracting fECG. The top figure shows the raw abdominal signal, which is a mix of background noise, mother ECG, and fECG. Like Method 1, the mother’s heart activity is the strongest part of the signal, which makes the fetal parts less visible. The middle plot depicts the thoracic signal taken from the mother’s chest. It has a clear mECG. This reference signal is very important for adaptive filtering to find and get rid of maternal signals from the abdominal recording. The last fECG taken using 342.Method 2 is shown in the bottom plot. In this scenario, the waveform has sharper and more obvious R-peaks with a larger amplitude than those obtained in Method 1. This suggests that Method 2 may use a more aggressive or improved way to separate signals. This could mean that the fetal signals are better isolated, but it could also mean that the signal reconstruction method had some amplification effects. However, the retrieved waveform clearly shows different fetal heart rhythms with less interference from the mother. The results show that Method 2 works to separate the fECG, which could be useful for later analysis like estimating the FHR and checking the health of the mother before birth.

Figure 15.7 shows how the R-peak detection procedure works on the fECG data that was taken out using Method 2. The blue waveform shows the final fECG signal after the mother’s parts were taken out and the signal was made stronger. The red marks show the recognized R-peaks, which are the places with the largest amplitude in each cardiac cycle. These are important for getting an accurate FHR. The R-peaks in Method 2 are sharper, clearer, and more pronounced than those in Method 1. This 343.means that Method 2 makes a cleaner and stronger fECG signal. The peak amplitude observed was more than 200 units, which could mean that the signal became clearer or that amplification was added during processing. The accurate and clear detection of R-peaks proves that Method 2 successfully separates fetal heart activity while keeping the shape of the heart intact for clinical evaluation and ongoing fetal surveillance.

344.Using eigenvalue analysis on 12 test cases, Figure 15.8 compares the SNR of Methods 1 and 2. The data show that Method 1 always gets higher SNR values, with big peaks in Cases 5 and 6, where the SNR is over 4.5 dB. This means that Method 1 is better at picking out the fECG signal while getting rid of any leftover maternal signals and noise. Method 2, on the other hand, is less reliable and works well in certain circumstances (like Case 6) but shows a big drop in SNR in others (like cases 9 345.and 10). This inconsistency suggests that Method 2 might not be as strong or useful for a wide range of subjects or signal situations.

Figure 15.9 shows the results of a cross-correlation analysis that was used to check SNR by comparing the extracted fECG signal to an ideal reference waveform. In Case 4, Method 1 again shows better performance, attaining a peak SNR of almost 3.5 dB and keeping high values over all test instances. This means that the fECG signals taken with Method 1 are not only cleaner, but they also match the real cardiac rhythm better, which is very important for getting an accurate estimate of the FHR. Method 2, on the other hand, gives SNR levels that are steadier but lower overall, usually between 2.7 and 2.9 dB. This shows that the baseline performance is stable, but it also shows that Method 2 has trouble getting high signal purity and synchronizing with actual fetal heart activity.

15.6 CONCLUSION

This study presents a hybrid approach for FHR estimation by integrating RLS adaptive filtering with SWT and two distinct denoising techniques. In Method 1, a threshold-based denoising algorithm is applied alongside RLS and SWT. In Method 2, SWT and RLS are combined with ISSNF algorithm. Both methods utilize the RLS algorithm within the wavelet domain after decomposing thoracic and abdominal 346.ECG signals via SWT. The proposed techniques effectively extract fECG signals, even in cases where maternal and fetal signals overlap. Experimental evaluation using R-peak detection and SNR analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of both methods. The threshold-based method (Method 1) proves advantageous in terms of computational efficiency and enhanced R-peak detection accuracy. Both denoising approaches, however, contribute significantly to the clarity and diagnostic reliability of the extracted signals. Subsequent application of a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier for fetal health assessment further validates the quality of the extracted signals. The classification results not only show improved accuracy but also reinforce the adaptability of the extraction pipeline. Overall, the proposed methodology outperforms traditional techniques in terms of signal quality, robustness, and diagnostic reliability.

348.16Heart Rate Estimation Using an Electrocardiogram-Aided Photoplethysmography Signal Quality Assessment Framework

K. Naga Sankar Reedy, Peddapullaiahgari Hariobulesu, Shaik Karimullah, Anwar Bhasha Pattan, and Fahimuddin Shaik

DOI: 10.1201/9781003634768-16

16.1 Introduction

A popular non-invasive optical technique for tracking variations in blood capacity within the microvascular cradle of tissue is photoplethysmography (PPG). It is essential to wearable medical technology because it makes it possible to track vital signs like blood oxygen saturation and heart rate in real time [1]. PPG works by outstanding light into the skin, usually red or infrared and measuring the light that is reflected or transmitted. The intensity of this light changes in response to the pulsating blood flow brought on by cardiac cycles. These changes in the PPG signal result in two components: the alternating current (AC) component, which is associated with the heartbeat and is associated primarily with physiological measures; and the direct current (DC) component, which is associated with the baseline blood volume and static tissue. The PPG signals from the wrist or fingertip are typically recorded in either transmissive or reflective mode. In insightful mode, the source and detector are both placed on the similar side of the muscle, while in transmissive mode, the light source travels through the tissue to the detector, which is located on the contradictory side of the source. Despite this convenience for use in wearable technology, the PPG signal is highly vulnerable to a number of artifacts, including motion artifacts, physiological anomalies, and ambient light. These noise sources can severely undercut the 349.eminence of the PPG signal, leading to erroneous physiological parameter estimation, such as heart rate [2].

A strong signal superiority assessment system is needed to address the ongoing problem of signals not being reliable. The signal quality assessment (SQA) methods have primarily depended on human annotators who use manual annotation, which are subjective and time consuming [3]. This leads to the incorporation of auxiliary signals, especially electrocardiography (ECG), an undeniable advantage in such a situation. The electrocardiogram records the electrical action of the heart and makes for a strong relay signal because the three different signals—the P wave, the QRS compound, and the T wave—are all connected to somewhat different physiological events in the cardiac cycle. Even with the distinct limitations of the ECG, which include issues such as baseline wander, electromyogram noise, and motion artifacts, the ECG still acts as the gold standard for cardiac-based measurement. An ECG-related PPG SQA system has the possibility to significantly improve the accuracy of PPG signal classification by leveraging the functional relationship between the ECG and also PPG [4]. In the method outlined, the PPG waveform features can be matched with the timing of cardiac events drawn from the ECG to separate high-quality signal segments from corrupted signal segments (Figure 16.1). Specifically, the time it takes for pulse transit time which lags among the R-peak of the ECG and the corresponding pulse of the PPG could be used to measure the synchrony and confirm PPG signal validity.

The integration of deep learning, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), adds an incredibly powerful new dimension to the assessment of signal quality. Neural networks, particularly approaches similar to AlexNet, enable high-accuracy automatic classification of signal quality by learning complex representations from PPG signal spectrogram images [5]. CNNs can find subtle patterns indicating motion corruption or noise because they can extract multiple hierarchical features from time-frequency representations. As this study intends to employ AlexNet to classify quality segments as “high quality,” only high-quality segments will be assessed for heart rate. After quality assessment, feature extraction is accomplished on the pre-processed 350.PPG waveforms to identify periodic peaks indicating cardiac cycles. Heart rate is derived from the inter-pulse intervals (IPIs); heart rate is determined as the reciprocal average of the IPI. When derived from methods of spectral analysis like the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), it is also possible to extract the dominant frequency that represents heart rate. To provide an additional layer of robustness, the validity of the heart rate derived from PPG required to be cross-validated against the heart rate derived from ECG signals [20].

The new proposed ECG-assisted SQA system offered superior performance against common heart rate estimation techniques (Figure 16.2). The ECG-assisted SQA offered an inferior mean absolute error (MAE) in heart rate estimates (1.699 vs. 1.901 bpm), and also had a higher rejection rate for poor-quality signals (0.816 vs. 0.776). These improvements to heart rate estimates illustrate the significant advantages of integrating more advanced neural network models of physiological knowledge in biomedical signal processing. Lastly, it increases the reliability of wearable health monitoring devices by ensuring that physiological assessment would only use high-quality PPG data.

16.2 LITERATURE REVIEW

The review of the literature also emphasizes how important data augmentation strategies can be to increase the amount and variety of training data to improve the performance of the deep learning model. It also emphasizes the need for standardized evaluation metrics that will allow them to compare the performance of the various strategies and ensure their research can be replicated. However, there is a need for future studies to recover the accuracy and reliability of PPG SQAs, and to do this, they can target unique architectures for deep learning, and apply their model consistently when using data augmentation. There are a myriad of articles that focus on incorporating deep learning for quality assessment of PPG One recent study offered an exciting new way of increasing accuracy by using multi-series scale data and multi-class features. They achieved the highest accuracy of 94.21%, and both learning and 351.decision rules in a hybrid model were used to assess the quality of PPG signals. In that model, learning and applying a trade-off between rule-based and learning-based methods appeared to be adequate for reliably evaluating signal quality. Additionally, a new method was applied that learned only a limited number of interpretable convolutional kernels and showed to demonstrate performance similar to a deep neural net while managing fewer parameters. On low-power devices, this technique enables effective, reliable, and interpretable signal quality evaluation.

Using a multi-scale CNN and bi- long short-term memory (LSTM), the authors combined multi-class features with multi-scale sequence data to propose a novel approach for evaluating the quality of PPG signals. When compared to other approaches, the suggested method’s accuracy of 94.21% was the highest. The use of deep learning for PPG SQA is not specifically mentioned in the paper. The study suggests a hybrid model for evaluating signal quality that blends learning and decision rules. To assist doctors in the process of continuous monitoring, a hybrid ResNet and bi-LSTM-based deep learning model [6] is suggested for the diagnosis of cardiovascular disease (CVDs) from PPG signals. Monte Carlo Dropout (MCD) and Bayesian optimization techniques are used in an assurance—conscious framework [7] for cuff-less blood pressure estimation. This framework performs better than simple MCD and yields more accurate predictions. AvgPool_VGG-16 is a novel approach that uses PPG signals and deep learning models [8] to classify the stages of hypertension. Additionally, to denoise a PPG signal, a hybrid approach that uses deep learning to take advantage of the wavelets’ multiresolution analysis capability is presented [9]. This study will define the optimal number of filters (16, 32, 64) and layers (2 and 4 layers) with the rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function, as well as assess the robustness of the trained CNN models utilized [12, 13] using hidden PPG datasets using varying noise. Wang et al. established a PPG based SQA method [10, 11] via a rare PPG signal and CNN while retaining optimal boundaries. Sukor et al.’s [14] study used an automated rejection method for artifact-contaminated PPG waveforms that examined waveform geomorphology and a choice tree classifier; however, the complexity of these studies was quite high. Li and Clifford [15] introduced a dynamic time warping (DTW) technique to stretch or shrink the single-cycle pulse waveform to fit the running template, which was combined with other signal quality indicators. Similarly, Couceiro et al. [16] introduced a motion artifact detection algorithm based on variation of time domain and period-domain features of PPG signals with a support vector machine (SVM) model. Cherif et al. [17] proposed a novel waveform morphology-based adaptive thresholding method utilizing a random alteration test to identify artifacts in PPG signals. Cherif et al. [17] presented a novel waveform morphology-based technique for adaptive thresholding that uses a random alteration test to identify artifacts in PPG signals. A 1-deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) model was shaped by Goh et al. [18] to classify five-second PPG sections as either clean or object-affected. CNN and SVM techniques were used by Liu et al. [19] to assess the characteristics of PPG indications from a wear forehead pulsation oximeter. Therefore, by adding more multi-class features, investigating various methods for extracting multi-scale series information, and testing the suggested approach on bigger and more varied datasets, these papers demonstrate the potential for future research in enhancing PPG SQA. For the evaluation of PPG signal quality, 352.they recommend more research into hybrid models that integrate learning and decision rules. This includes creating increasingly complex decision rules and examining various combinations of learning and rule-based methodologies.

16.3 PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

Using an optical sensing system to acquire PPG signals is the first step in the methodology for assessing the quality of PPG signals. This device is applied to the fingertip and usually consists of a photodetector and a light-emitting diode (LED). The light that the LED emits enters the skin and interacts with the blood vessels underneath. The amount of light engrossed is changed by the volume of blood in these vessels as the heart contracts and relaxes in its normal rhythm. Blood volume rises during systole, absorbing light and lowering the amount of light that reaches the detector. On the other hand, as blood volume drops during diastole, more light can be seen. The raw PPG waveform is created by converting these variations in light absorption into an analog signal.

A series of periodic pulses with a diastolic valley and a systolic peak each make up this waveform. The diastolic valley shows the lowest blood volume and the highest detected light, while the systolic peak represents the maximum blood volume and the lowest point of detected light intensity. However, motion artifacts, ambient light disturbances, and incorrect sensor positioning can all degrade the quality of the raw PPG signal. Preprocessing techniques, such as high-pass or band-pass filtering (usually within 0.5–5 Hz) to remove slowly varying noise from motion or respiration, are used to address this. Additionally, normalization is used to control amplitude variations brought on by variations in finger structure, skin tone, or sensor location.

After preprocessing the signal, heart rate is estimated by locating the systolic peaks and figuring out the IPIs—the times between consecutive peaks. Based on these intervals, the heart rate is calculated in beats per minute. To improve reliability, dominant frequency components are identified through spectral analysis using the STFT, providing a frequency-based method for heart rate estimation. However, the excellence of the input PPG signals has a significant impact on this process’ accuracy.

16.3.1 Training Stage

An ECG SQA mechanism is presented to increase the accuracy of heart rate readings (Figure 16.3). ECG signals, which include distinct waveforms like the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave, offer a trustworthy electrical record of the heart’s activity. The physiological timing between electrical and mechanical cardiac events causes the R-peaks in the ECG to line up with the matching features in the PPG waveform, synchronization with the ECG is assessed using this alignment as a guide. The PPG segment is flagged as low quality and not processed further if it is discordant or shows noticeable deviation. By ensuring that only precise, high-integrity segments are used, this cross-validation with ECG data improves the SQA system’s resilience.

353.16.3.2 Proposed CNN Architecture

The system uses CNNs to automate this evaluation, with AlexNet acting as the central model (Figure 16.4). To create two-dimensional (2D) images that retain both time and frequency information, the PPG signals are first transformed into time-frequency spectrograms using STFT. After being fed these spectrogram images, the CNN learns to recognize patterns that differentiate high-quality signals from low-quality ones. The CNN has been trained to identify minute distortions or noise characteristics that conventional filtering methods might miss. Consequently, the system gains the ability to generalize across a wide range of topics and circumstances, which makes it useful in practical applications.

With an input layer, multiple convolutional layers (CLs), pooling layers, a fully connected (FC) layer, and an output layer, the CNN functions as a feed-forward network. By applying filters to the input data, the CLs serve as feature extractors, identifying key characteristics and patterns in the STFT images. Pooling layers, also known as max-pooling, are used after each convolution to lower the dimensionality of the 354.feature maps and preserve only the most pertinent data. By randomly turning off specific neurons during training, dropout layers help the network avoid overfitting and improve the model’s ability to simplify to new data.

In these layers, the ReLU serves as the main activation function because it can effectively introduce non-linearity, which helps the model learn intricate patterns. All of the extracted features are compiled by the last decision layer, an FC layer, which then employs a sigmoid activation function to produce a probability score ranging from 0 to 1. This score makes binary classification easier by indicating the probability that the input PPG signal falls into a high-quality or low-quality category.

The ECG, PPG signals are processed concurrently in the ECG-guided architecture. After passing ECG signals through an R-peak detection module, the R–R intervals are used to calculate heart rate. CNN uses this heart rate as a guide when classifying the PPG segments. Before the PPG signal is fed into the CNN, it goes through preprocessing, feature extraction, and transformation into STFT images in parallel. The system makes sure that only trustworthy PPG segments are used for heart rate estimation by comparing the CNN classification results with the reference that was obtained from the ECG.

Various metrics such as MAE, root mean square error (RMSE), and correlation coefficients can be used to evaluate the CNN models. The metrics define the extent to which the prompted heart rate from the PPG conforms to the heart rate from the electrocardiogram (ECG) reference. Based on the experimental results, the ECG-referenced SQA system is more efficient in eliminating noise from the signals and provides a lower error rate than the standalone PPG analysis methods. In conclusion, this integrated system provides a reliable and scalable solution for accurately monitoring heart rate in wearable healthcare applications by combining optical sensing, signal processing, deep learning, and validation from the ECG.

16.4 DATA COLLECTION

The evaluation of PPG signal quality is fundamental to accurately monitor blood flow and cardiovascular health. Traditional approaches require human review, which can be tedious and not always accurate. CNNs leveraged a deep learning approach to classify PPG signals as high quality or low quality automatically to overcome this problem (Figure 16.5). The investigators utilized the Vital DB database, a publicly available database of vital signs for surgical patients. PPG signals for 200 people were taken at a sampling rate of 125 Hz with a finger sensor (SNUADC device). From this data, 5,804 signal segments were chosen; 3,969 of these were classified as high quality, and 1,835 as low quality. ECG signals served as a reference for the expert review that produced these labels. Uncertain or difficult-to-classify signals were eliminated. Eighty percent of the participant data was used for training, and 20% was used for testing.

16.4.1 Data Preparation

Each 10-second PPG signal segment was transformed into a 2D image using the STFT to prepare the data for the CNN. By displaying the signal’s frequency variation 355.over time, STFT facilitates CNN’s ability to identify patterns. The frequency range was set between 0 and 8 Hz, and a Hanning window of size 256 was employed. The size of the resulting STFT images was 250 × 334 pixels. The CNN, which was trained to identify patterns that indicate whether the signal was of good or bad quality, was fed these images. Signals of high quality matched the ECG heart rate well and had distinct shapes. Signals with poor quality contained noise, hazy patterns, or heart rates that did not match. The ability of the trained CNN model to distinguish between good and bad signals was then evaluated using fresh data. With this technique, PPG signal checking becomes quicker, more reliable, and appropriate for use in real-time health monitoring systems such as hospital equipment or wearables.

16.5 SIMULATION AND RESULTS

Performance metrics are important for evaluating a model’s performance. They help determine a model’s accuracy, efficiency, and reliability for completing its task. Evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score show how good a model can classify or group in classification problems. Accuracy or number of correct predictions may not be of great use if one class is strongly dominant. Precision, the number of correct positive comparisons the model made when false positives are a problem, measures the proportion of the model’s positive predictions that are correct. Recall, which is sometimes referred to as sensitivity, the number of positive cases the model correctly identified, will be a concerned metrics in applications such as fraud detection and healthcare. The F1-score will provide a reasonable summary of recall and precision. Specificity monitors how well the model detects negative cases. By utilizing all of these important metrics, developers will have a better view of their model performance and note issues such as overfitting or bias, to improve the model. This research will compare the performance of traditional machine learning models and the proposed deep learning model. We will use Histogram of Oriented Gradients 356.(HOG) to extract features from 2D STFT images of PPG signals is a common feature extraction strategy used to perceive salient patterns from datasets. Three machine learning models—the random forest (RF), SVM, and multilayer perceptron (MLP)—are then trained using these features. MATLAB 2023a is used to analyze 1,764 HOG features that are extracted from each PPG signal image. The original PPG waveform is also used to test a 1D CNN to provide a fair comparison. The 2D CNN model used in this study, which operates on STFT spectrograms, outperforms the MLP, RF, and SVM models, according to performance results in Table 16.1. It exhibits improved metrics. The advantage of employing STFT-based spectrograms and CNNs for precise PPG SQA is further supported by the 2D CNN model’s marginally better performance than the 1D CNN model.

16.5.1 Confusion Matrix

The binary classification model’s ability to discriminate between “Good” and “Bad” PPG signals is detailed in the confusion matrix displayed in Figure 16.6. There are four significant values in it: false positives (FP = 31), in which a “Bad” signal is mistakenly predicted to be “Good,” false negatives (FN = 10), in which a “Good” signal is mistakenly classified as “Bad,” true positives (TP = 437), in which the model correctly identifies a “Good” signal; and true negatives (TN = 174). The model’s ability to accurately classify both signal types is demonstrated by the high TP and TN values. The comparatively low FP and FN values indicate that the model performs well overall and is reliable in determining the quality of PPG signals.

To assess classification performance and pinpoint areas for development, it is crucial to calculate key performance metrics, which are made possible by this confusion matrix.

16.5.2 Estimation of Heart Rate ECG versus PPG

Figure 16.7 displays a comparison of heart rate data over a time of 400 seconds using PPG and ECG. As the reference standard for heart rate, the ECG signal is represented by a solid blue line and remains comparatively constant. Conversely, the PPG heart rate signal represented in red, indicates differences over its duration, which shows the PPG signals are more reliable to noise, motion artifacts, or outside influences that may compromise heart rate accuracy. Despite this comparison revealing the limitations of 357.using PPG-based monitoring and reaffirming the importance of using robust methods of signal processing and quality assessment, it is encouraged to make PPG-based monitoring more reproducible and reliable in real-world situations.

16.6 CONCLUSION

This research provides a thorough lean framework for heart rate estimation from PPG signals by implementing an ECG-aided SQA system. This approach identified bits of low-quality PPG portions and eliminated them before heart rate estimation. Specifically, the approach to tackling this presented research employed STFT-transformed PPG spectrograms classified using AlexNet, a deep CNN, MAE, and RMSE improvements indicate that the process guarantees better performance, reliability, and lower error by linking the heart rates collected and derived from PPG versus ECG, which no one argues is the “gold standard.”

The system’s accuracy and reliability are driven by the data engineered through a deep learning-based model that provides automated, data-driven classification when compared to conventional rule-based SQA that was traditionally used for PPG signal quality. A dataset comprising 600 seconds of continuous PPG recordings from 102 individuals is used to thoroughly validate the efficacy of the suggested method. With 358.98.3% accuracy, 98.9% sensitivity, 96.7% specificity, and an F1 score of 98.8%, the model performs admirably.

These findings support the possibility of using physiological signal cross-validation in conjunction with deep learning to provide more reliable heart rate monitoring. This kind of integration could be particularly helpful in clinical settings and wearable technology, allowing for more reliable and accurate real-time health monitoring.
